### Assistant

Game of Active Directory (GOAD) is an intentionally vulnerable Active Directory environment designed to give you a safe, realistic network to practice attack techniques and defense strategies. For a thesis focusing on AD security, it provides an excellent, repeatable proving ground.While GOAD can run on VirtualBox, VMware Workstation Pro is highly recommended on Windows for a stable experience with complex AD environments. The latest versions of GOAD have moved to a Python-based orchestrator, making native Windows installation much smoother.1Install PrerequisitesHypervisor, Vagrant, Python, and Git1.Install Prerequisites:Hypervisor, Vagrant, Python, and Git.You will need several core tools installed on your Windows machine:VMware Workstation Pro: Ensure virtualization is enabled in your BIOS and disable conflicting hypervisors like Hyper-V.Vagrant & Vagrant VMware Utility: Download Vagrant from HashiCorp. Crucially, you must also install the Vagrant VMware Utility — without it, Vagrant cannot bridge communications with VMware.Python: Install Python 3.11 or newer. Make sure to check the "Add Python to PATH" box during installation.Git: Install Git for Windows to clone the repository.2Install Required Vagrant Plugins2.Install Required Vagrant Plugins:GOAD relies on Vagrant plugins to handle Windows-based provisioning via WinRM and handle automatic reboots. Open a terminal (PowerShell or Command Prompt) and run:Bashvagrant plugin install vagrant-vmware-desktop winrm winrm-fs winrm-elevated vagrant-reload
3Clone the GOAD Repository3.Clone the GOAD Repository:Download the official GOAD repository which contains all the configuration files and automation scripts:Bashgit clone https://github.com/Orange-Cyberdefense/GOAD
cd GOAD
4Install Python Dependencies4.Install Python Dependencies:GOAD relies on several Python libraries to execute its Ansible playbooks. It is highly recommended to do this inside a virtual environment to avoid conflicting with your system Python:Bashpython -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
5Deploy and Provision the LabThis step can take several hours depending on your hardware5.Deploy and Provision the Lab:This step can take several hours depending on your hardware.With the virtual environment active, run the Python orchestration script to build the VMs and provision the Active Directory forest. For a full VMware deployment, use:Bashpython goad.py -t install -l GOAD -p vmware -m local
Note: If your computer has limited resources (less than 32GB RAM), you can replace -l GOAD with -l GOAD-Light to deploy a smaller, 3-VM version of the lab instead of the full 5-VM architecture.Testing GOAD for Your ThesisOnce the lab is running, it acts as a black-box environment full of real-world misconfigurations. A typical testing methodology for your thesis might follow these phases:Reconnaissance & Enumeration: Use tools like nmap or CrackMapExec (or NetExec) to scan the lab's subnet, locate the Domain Controllers, and identify exposed services (like LDAP, SMB, and Kerberos).Domain Mapping: Deploy BloodHound to visualize the Active Directory environment. By running SharpHound or a Python equivalent to collect data, you can map out user-group memberships, ACLs, and uncover hidden attack paths (e.g., users with ForceChangePassword rights over other accounts).Exploitation: Test specific AD vulnerabilities that are intentionally baked into GOAD. Common scenarios include Kerberoasting, AS-REP Roasting, SMB relay attacks, or exploiting overly permissive certificate templates (ADCS).Post-Exploitation: Once you compromise a high-privileged account or a Domain Admin, you can test persistence mechanisms by extracting credentials using DCSync (via Mimikatz) or generating a Golden Ticket.To refine your thesis approach:Compare GOAD vs GOAD-Light architecturesWalk me through a BloodHound AD mappingFree Active Directory Pentesting Lab Setup: GOAD
This walkthrough demonstrates the foundational setup process and highlights the specific misconfigurations you can target during your thesis testing.

### Assistant

Good catch uploading those screenshots. I can see exactly what's causing the headache—and it's a software conflict, not something you did wrong!In your second screenshot, you are running VMware Workstation Pro 26H1. This is a very recent release from Broadcom, and unfortunately, the HashiCorp vagrant-vmware-utility installer currently has a known compatibility bug with it.The Root CauseThe Vagrant utility installer is hardcoded to look for specific Windows registry keys and installation paths that were standard in VMware Workstation 17.x and earlier. Because Broadcom changed some of the underlying installation structure and registry footprint in the 26H1 release, the Vagrant installer goes completely blind. It assumes VMware isn't installed at all, triggering that exact warning dialog you are seeing.The Fix: Drop back to 17.5.xBecause you are setting up GOAD for your thesis, you want the most stable infrastructure possible. Fighting hypervisor compatibility bugs will just eat into your actual security research time.Here is the most reliable path forward:Uninstall 26H1: Go into your Windows Apps & Features and uninstall this version of VMware Workstation.Install the 17.x Stable Release: Download and install the latest stable VMware Workstation Pro 17.5.x branch instead. (Note: Broadcom recently made Workstation Pro completely free for personal and educational use, so you can easily grab the standard 17.5 installer without needing a new license). 3. Re-run the Vagrant Utility: Launch the vagrant-vmware-utility setup file again. It will instantly recognize the v17 registry keys and install successfully.Once that utility installs, it will quietly run as a background service. From there, your terminal won't throw those connection errors anymore, and you'll be fully cleared to run the Python orchestration script to build your Active Directory lab.

### Assistant

Ah, that is a classic GOAD curveball! You didn't do anything wrong; the documentation on many blogs is just slightly outdated.The GOAD developers recently updated how they manage dependencies. They completely removed the standard requirements.txt file and combined their Python (pip) dependencies and Ansible dependencies into the same YAML files.Because of this, pip is actually expecting you to feed it one of those .yml files instead. Which one you use depends entirely on your Python version.Here is how to get past this error:1. Check your Python VersionFirst, check which version of Python your virtual environment is running:DOSpython --version
2. Run the Correct Pip CommandBased on your version, run the corresponding command while your (.venv) is still active:If you have Python 3.11 or newer:DOSpip install -r requirements_311.yml
If you have Python 3.8 to 3.10:DOSpip install -r requirements.yml
(Note: It might feel weird running a .yml file through pip, but the GOAD developers specifically formatted those files so both pip and ansible-galaxy can read them!)3. Install the Ansible Galaxy RequirementsOnce pip finishes installing the Python tools (like ansible-core and pywinrm), you need to pull down the Ansible collections that actually configure the Active Directory domain.Run this command next (again, matching the file to your Python version):DOScd ansible
ansible-galaxy install -r requirements_311.yml 
(Or use requirements.yml if on an older Python version)..After that finishes, use cd .. to go back to the main GOAD folder, and you will be ready to launch the python goad.py deployment script!

### Assistant

The "Ansible on Windows" WallThis is a rite of passage for everyone setting up GOAD on Windows! You did nothing wrong, and the installation of the Python packages actually worked perfectly.The issue is that Ansible is completely incompatible with native Windows. While pip allows you to install the ansible-core package, the moment you attempt to execute a command like ansible-galaxy or ansible-playbook, it crashes. That [WinError 1] Incorrect function error is Ansible attempting to use a Unix-specific file-system check (os.get_blocking()) that standard Windows command prompts simply do not have.How to Fix This for Your LabGOAD deployments consist of two distinct phases:Infrastructure: Building the VMs (Vagrant + VMware).Provisioning: Turning those blank VMs into a vulnerable Active Directory domain (Ansible).Because you are on Windows, you cannot use the goad.py script to do both at the same time. You must split the process: build the VMs in Windows, then provision them using Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL).Here is your new deployment path:Phase 1: Build the VMs (On Windows)Stay in your current Windows Command Prompt. Bypass the goad.py script and launch Vagrant directly to build the blank virtual machines.Navigate to the specific provider directory for your lab:DOScd ad\GOAD\providers\vmware
Start the VM build process:DOSvagrant up
(This will take a while. Let Vagrant download the base boxes and spin up the 5 VMs in VMware).Phase 2: Provision AD (On WSL)Once the VMs are running in VMware, you must switch to a Linux environment to run the Ansible configuration.Open your Start Menu, type Ubuntu (or your preferred WSL distro), and open the Linux terminal. (If you do not have WSL installed, open an admin PowerShell and run wsl --install, then reboot).Inside WSL, clone the GOAD repository again:Bashgit clone https://github.com/Orange-Cyberdefense/GOAD
cd GOAD
Set up a Python virtual environment inside Linux:Bashpython3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements_311.yml
Install the Ansible Galaxy collections (this will now work!):Bashcd ansible
ansible-galaxy install -r requirements_311.yml
Finally, run the Ansible playbook to configure the Active Directory domain across the running VMs:Bashansible-playbook -i ../ad/GOAD/data/inventory -i ../ad/GOAD/providers/vmware/inventory main.yml
By letting Windows handle the heavy lifting of VMware virtualization, and letting WSL handle the Ansible network configuration, you bypass the compatibility errors entirely.

Ah, I see exactly what happened! You hit another layer of GOAD's custom architecture.You cannot run vagrant up manually inside that providers/vmware directory. If you open that Vagrantfile, you will see it relies on Ruby code that expects specific environment variables and data from a config.json file. When you run vagrant up by itself, Vagrant doesn't know what VMs to build, what IP addresses to assign, or what OS "box" to use, resulting in that A box must be specified error.You must use the goad.py orchestrator to build the VMs, but we will tell it to only build the VMs and stop before it triggers the Windows-incompatible Ansible step.Here is how to get the VMs building:Step 1: Return to the Root GOAD DirectoryIn your Windows command prompt, back out of those nested folders until you are in the main GOAD directory where goad.py lives.DOScd C:\Users\hs32\Desktop\GOAD
Step 2: Build the VMs (Without Provisioning)We are going to use the goad.py script, but instead of the full install command, we will use the build action. This tells the Python script to read all the configurations, pass them to Vagrant, and spin up the VMs in VMware, but skip the Ansible phase.Run this command:DOSpython goad.py -t build -l GOAD -p vmware
(If you get a prompt asking about installing missing Python modules, hit enter or accept it).You should immediately see Vagrant start pulling down the Windows Server boxes (which are large, usually around 5-6GB each) and booting them inside VMware Workstation.Step 3: Switch to WSL for ProvisioningOnce all 5 VMs are fully booted and running in the background, leave VMware running.Now, open your Ubuntu (WSL) terminal and do the Ansible phase:Clone the repo and prep the Python environment inside Linux (just like you did on Windows):Bashgit clone https://github.com/Orange-Cyberdefense/GOAD
cd GOAD
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements_311.yml
cd ansible
ansible-galaxy install -r requirements_311.yml
Run the Ansible provisioning playbook manually from within the ansible directory:Bashansible-playbook -i ../ad/GOAD/data/inventory -i ../ad/GOAD/providers/vmware/inventory main.yml
The script will reach out over the virtual network to the VMs you built in Windows and begin configuring Active Directory!

You've hit a classic Python version compatibility bug! You did absolutely nothing wrong.You are using Python 3.14, and in recent versions of Python, the configparser module became much stricter. It now instantly crashes if a script tries to write an .ini file where a key contains a colon (:) or an equals sign (=).When you ran goad.py for the first time, it noticed you didn't have a configuration file yet. It tried to auto-generate one with helpful comments in the keys (like ; lab: goad...), but Python saw that colon, threw an InvalidWriteError, and panicked.The Fix: Bypass the Auto-GeneratorWe can easily bypass this buggy code block by manually creating the configuration file so the script doesn't try to do it for you.1. Create the configuration file manually
Run this command in your active (.venv) prompt to open a blank file in Notepad:DOSnotepad C:\Users\hs32\.goad\goad.ini
(If it asks if you want to create a new file, click Yes).2. Paste in the minimal configuration
Copy the text below exactly as is, paste it into Notepad, save the file, and close Notepad:Ini, TOML[default]
lab = GOAD
provider = vmware
3. Run the build command again
Now that the goad.ini file exists, the script will skip the create_config_file() function and actually start building your lab! Run your command one more time:DOSpython goad.py -t build -l GOAD -p vmware
You should see Vagrant take over and start pulling down the Windows Server images. Let me know when the VMs are up in VMware!

### Assistant

Ah, the classic "Clash of the Hypervisors"!Remember earlier when we ran wsl --install so we could use Ubuntu for the Ansible phase? That command automatically turned on Microsoft's hidden virtualization engine (Hyper-V). VMware is basically throwing its hands up and saying, "I can't start this VM because Microsoft is already hogging the CPU's virtualization features!"Because you are using a modern version of VMware Workstation (17.x), it actually can coexist peacefully with WSL and Hyper-V, but Windows requires one extra bridge feature to be enabled so they can share the hardware.Here is how to make them play nice:Step 1: Enable the Windows Hypervisor PlatformThis is the official Microsoft API that allows third-party apps (like VMware) to run on top of Hyper-V.Open your Windows Start Menu, type PowerShell, right-click it, and select Run as Administrator.Paste in this exact command and hit Enter:PowerShellEnable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName HypervisorPlatform -All
Windows will install the feature. If it asks you to restart your computer, type Y and restart. (If it doesn't ask, restart your computer anyway just to be safe).Step 2: Disable Nested Virtualization on the VMVagrant boxes sometimes try to enable "nested virtualization" (the ability to run a VM inside a VM). When Hyper-V is running on the host machine, VMware cannot pass nested virtualization through to the guest. The GOAD VMs do not actually need this feature, so we can just turn it off.Open VMware Workstation Pro.Click on the GOAD-DC01 machine in your library (the one we opened earlier).Click Edit virtual machine settings.On the left side, click on Processors.On the right side, look under the "Virtualization engine" section. Uncheck the box that says Virtualize Intel VT-x/EPT or AMD-V/RVI.Click OK.Step 3: Power It On!Now, click Power on this virtual machine directly in the VMware GUI.It should successfully boot up into a standard Windows Server login screen!If it boots successfully, power it back off from the GUI. Then, open your command prompt, go back to your C:\Users\hs32\Desktop\GOAD\workspace\57aa65-goad-vmware\provider folder, and run vagrant up again. It will now successfully boot DC01 and move on to building the other 4 machines!

While GOAD can run on VirtualBox, VMware Workstation Pro is highly recommended on Windows for a stable experience with complex AD environments. You will need several core tools installed on your Windows machine:  VMware Workstation Pro: Ensure virtualization is enabled in your BIOS and disable conflicting hypervisors like Hyper-V. Crucially, you must also install the Vagrant VMware Utility — without it, Vagrant cannot bridge communications with VMware.  https://developer.hashicorp.com/vagrant/install  Note: Vagrant utility might not support latest versions of Vmware.  so, install a stable version like: 17.6  activate with license keys from following: https://github.com/hegdepavankumar/VMware-Workstation-Pro-17-Licence-Keys  Python: Install Python 3.11 or newer. Make sure to check the "Add Python to PATH" box during installation.  Git: Install Git for Windows to clone the repository.  2. Install Required Vagrant Plugins  GOAD relies on Vagrant plugins to handle Windows-based provisioning via WinRM and handle automatic reboots. Open a terminal (PowerShell or Command Prompt) and run:  vagrant plugin install vagrant-vmware-desktop winrm winrm-fs winrm-elevated vagrant-reload  3. Clone the GOAD Repository  Download the official GOAD repository which contains all the configuration files and automation scripts:  git clone <https://github.com/Orange-Cyberdefense/GOAD>  cd GOAD  4. Install Python Dependencies  GOAD relies on several Python libraries to execute its Ansible playbooks. It is highly recommended to do this inside a virtual environment to avoid conflicting with your system Python:  Bash  python -m venv .venv  .venv\\Scripts\\activate  Check your Python Version  First, check which version of Python your virtual environment is running:  python --version  Run the Correct Pip Command  Based on your version, run the corresponding command while your (.venv) is still active:  If you have Python 3.11 or newer:  pip install -r requirements_311.yml  If you have Python 3.8 to 3.10:  pip install -r requirements.yml  (Note: It might feel weird running a .yml file through pip, but the GOAD developers specifically formatted those files so both pip and ansible-galaxy can read them!))  5. Deploy and Provision the Lab  Step 1: Return to the Root GOAD Directory  In your Windows command prompt, back out of those nested folders until you are in the main GOAD directory where goad.py lives.  DOS  cd C:\\Users\\hs32\\Desktop\\GOAD  Step 2: Build the VMs (Without Provisioning)  We are going to use the goad.py script, but instead of the full install command, we will use the build action. This tells the Python script to read all the configurations, pass them to Vagrant, and spin up the VMs in VMware, but skip the Ansible phase.  Run this command:  DOS  python goad.py -t build -l GOAD -p vmware  (If you get a prompt asking about installing missing Python modules, hit enter or accept it). This step can take several hours depending on your hardware.  With the virtual environment active, run the Python orchestration script to build the VMs and provision the Active Directory forest. For a full VMware deployment, use:  python goad.py -t install -l GOAD -p vmware -m local  Note: If your computer has limited resources (less than 32GB RAM), you can replace -l GOAD with -l GOAD-Light to deploy a smaller, 3-VM version of the lab instead of the full 5-VM architecture.  Testing GOAD for Your Thesis  Once the lab is running, it acts as a black-box environment full of real-world misconfigurations. A typical testing methodology for your thesis might follow these phases:  Reconnaissance & Enumeration: Use tools like nmap or CrackMapExec (or NetExec) to scan the lab's subnet, locate the Domain Controllers, and identify exposed services (like LDAP, SMB, and Kerberos).  Domain Mapping: Deploy BloodHound to visualize the Active Directory environment. By running SharpHound or a Python equivalent to collect data, you can map out user-group memberships, ACLs, and uncover hidden attack paths (e.g., users with ForceChangePassword rights over other accounts).  Exploitation: Test specific AD vulnerabilities that are intentionally baked into GOAD. Common scenarios include Kerberoasting, AS-REP Roasting, SMB relay attacks, or exploiting overly permissive certificate templates (ADCS).  Post-Exploitation: Once you compromise a high-privileged account or a Domain Admin, you can test persistence mechanisms by extracting credentials using DCSync (via Mimikatz) or generating a Golden Ticket.  Free Active Directory Pentesting Lab Setup: GOAD  This walkthrough demonstrates the foundational setup process and highlights the specific misconfigurations you can target during your thesis testing.

### Assistant

This is a very standard Ubuntu quirk! Unlike Windows, Ubuntu does not include the Python virtual environment builder (venv) or the package manager (pip) by default in order to keep the operating system extremely lightweight.Because the very first command (python3 -m venv .venv) failed, the .venv folder was never properly created. That caused a domino effect where every subsequent command—like source, pip, and ansible-galaxy—also failed because they rely on that environment existing.Here is how to get your WSL environment prepped and back on track:1. Install the Missing Ubuntu PackagesFirst, you need to update Ubuntu's package list and install the missing Python tools using the apt package manager. Run these two commands:Bashsudo apt update
sudo apt install python3-venv python3-pip -y
(It will ask for your WSL Linux password. When you type it, no characters will show up on the screen—this is normal Linux security. Just type it and hit Enter).2. Delete the Broken EnvironmentWhen the first command crashed, it left behind a corrupted, empty .venv folder. You must delete it before trying again:Bashrm -rf .venv
3. Rebuild and ActivateNow that Ubuntu has the right tools, you can successfully recreate the isolated Python environment and activate it:Bashpython3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
(You will know it worked when your terminal prompt changes to include (.venv) at the beginning).4. Install the DependenciesNow that you are safely inside the virtual environment, pip and ansible will work perfectly. Run the rest of the GOAD setup commands:Bashpip install -r requirements_311.yml
Once that finishes, move into the ansible folder and pull down the collections:Bashcd ansible
ansible-galaxy install -r requirements_311.yml
5. Launch the ProvisioningWith all the prerequisites finally installed in WSL, you can execute the command to configure your running VMs.Make sure your Windows VMs are still powered on in VMware, then run:Bashansible-playbook -i ../workspace/57aa65-goad-vmware/inventory_disable_vagrant -i ../workspace/57aa65-goad-vmware/inventory main.yml

Phase 2: Provisioning Active Directory via WSL

Once all 5 VMs are fully booted in VMware, leave them running in the background. It is time to configure the vulnerable domain.

1. Open your Ubuntu (WSL) terminal.
2. Clone the GOAD repository inside Linux and prepare the virtual environment:

### What to do now:
Let the terminal sit and run. The initial setup tasks (installing components, pushing binaries, changing configurations, and setting up the trust relationships) will take anywhere from **1 to 2.5 hours** depending on your CPU and drive speeds. 

Once it finishes, it will print a `PLAY RECAP` showing all hosts with green or cyan status changes and zero failed tasks. At that point, your domain is live and fully ready for your security testing!

You have reached the final boss of the Windows GOAD deployment: The WSL-to-VMware Network Bridge.The error ConnectTimeoutError on port 5986 means your Ansible script (living inside WSL) is trying to send configuration commands to your Windows VMs over WinRM (Windows Remote Management), but the packets are dropping into a black hole.There are only two reasons this happens at this exact stage.Culprit 1: Vagrant Didn't FinishIn our previous troubleshooting steps, I mentioned powering on DC01 manually in the VMware GUI to bypass the Hyper-V error, and then powering it off so you could run vagrant up again.Did you run vagrant up in the Windows command prompt, and did it successfully complete for all 5 VMs?If you only powered them on via the VMware GUI, Vagrant never got the chance to run its internal setup scripts. A raw Windows Server image does not have WinRM enabled by default. Vagrant must inject the SSH keys, create the background user, and open port 5986 before Ansible can do its job.The Fix: If you didn't let vagrant up finish completely, close WSL, go back to your Windows Command Prompt in the workspace\57aa65-goad-vmware\provider folder, and run vagrant up. Let it run until it returns you to the prompt.Culprit 2: The Windows Firewall Block (Most Likely)If vagrant up did finish successfully and the VMs are sitting idle in VMware, you are hitting a classic Windows 10/WSL2 architecture quirk.WSL2 operates inside its own hidden network (usually a 172.x.x.x subnet). Your VMware VMs operate on a host-only network (the 192.168.56.x subnet). When WSL tries to talk to VMware, the traffic must route through your Windows host machine. Because Windows sees the WSL network adapter as an "Unidentified Public Network," the Windows Defender Firewall automatically blocks the traffic for security reasons.The Fix: We need to tell the Windows Firewall to trust traffic coming from your WSL terminal.Open your Windows Start Menu, type PowerShell, right-click it, and select Run as Administrator.Paste in this exact command and hit Enter:PowerShellNew-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow WSL" -Direction Inbound -InterfaceAlias "vEthernet (WSL)" -Action Allow
You should see a green block of text confirming the rule was created.Test and ResumeTo verify the bridge is working, go into your Ubuntu (WSL) terminal and try to ping the first Domain Controller:Bashping 192.168.56.10
(Press Ctrl + C to stop the ping).If you get replies instead of a timeout, your network bridge is fixed! Re-run your exact ansible-playbook command:Bashansible-playbook -i /mnt/c/Users/hs32/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/57aa65-goad-vmware/inventory_disable_vagrant -i /mnt/c/Users/hs32/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/57aa65-goad-vmware/inventory main.yml

### Assistant

This is the ultimate final boss of building GOAD on Windows, and you have run head-first into the "WSL2 NAT Boundary."Here is exactly what is happening: vagrant up did its job. Your 5 VMs are sitting happily in VMware on a private network (192.168.56.x). However, Windows Subsystem for Linux (Version 2) actually runs inside its own hidden Hyper-V virtual machine behind a NAT router.WSL2 literally does not have a physical or virtual route to reach VMware's private network adapters. It is sending those pings out, and Windows is dropping them because it refuses to route traffic between two different hypervisors.We are going to use a brilliant, native Windows trick to completely bypass this network boundary.The Fix: The WSL1 Network CollapseInstead of fighting Windows IP routing tables and firewall rules, we are going to temporarily downgrade your Ubuntu environment from WSL2 to WSL1.WSL1 does not use a virtual machine. It runs directly on the Windows kernel, which means it shares your host Windows network stack perfectly. The moment you switch to WSL1, Ubuntu will magically be able to see everything VMware sees.Step 1: Verify the VMs are alive (Sanity Check)
First, open your standard Windows Command Prompt (not Ubuntu) and ping the Domain Controller to ensure Vagrant actually gave it the right IP:DOSping 192.168.56.10
(You should get replies here. If you get a timeout in Windows too, let me know, because that means Vagrant failed to configure the network adapter).Step 2: Convert Ubuntu to WSL1
If the Windows ping was successful, leave your command prompt open and run this command to shut down the Linux subsystem:DOSwsl --shutdown
Now, convert your Ubuntu distro to version 1. (This process takes a minute or two and will not delete your GOAD files):DOSwsl --set-version Ubuntu 1
Step 3: Verify the Bridge
Once the conversion says "Operation successful," open your Ubuntu terminal again. Because it just rebooted, you need to reactivate your Python environment:Bashcd ~/GOAD/ansible
source ../.venv/bin/activate
Now, try that ping again from inside Linux:Bashping 192.168.56.10
You will immediately see successful replies! Press Ctrl + C to stop the ping, and hit the up arrow to run your ansible-playbook command one last time. It will connect to port 5986 and begin building your domain.

This timeout is actually incredibly helpful! It tells us exactly where the chain is broken.The problem is not WSL. Your host Windows machine cannot even see the virtual machine. If Windows can't see the VM, there is no way Ubuntu can route traffic to it.When you use Vagrant with VMware, Vagrant attempts to create a custom, hidden virtual network switch (usually called VMnet2 or similar) dedicated to the 192.168.56.x subnet. If this ping failed, it means one of three things happened: Vagrant failed to create the switch, the VM failed to grab the IP, or Windows classified the new switch as a "Public Network" and firewalled it.Let's find the break and fix it.Step 1: Check the Windows Side (The Virtual Switch)First, we need to see if Windows actually has a gateway to that network.In your Windows Command Prompt, type:DOSipconfig
Scroll through the output and look for your VMware Network Adapters.Do you see any adapter that has an IPv4 Address starting with 192.168.56... (usually 192.168.56.1)?If you DO NOT see it: Vagrant failed to create the virtual network. We will need to fix VMware's Virtual Network Editor.
If you DO see it: The switch exists, but the VM didn't connect to it properly. Proceed to Step 2.Step 2: Check the VM Side (Did it get the IP?)Sometimes the VM boots up so fast that Vagrant misses the window to inject the static IP address, leaving the VM with a dead network connection.Open the VMware Workstation GUI.Click on GOAD-DC01.Click inside the VM window and log in.
(The default Vagrant username is vagrant and the password is vagrant).Once you are on the Windows Server desktop, click the Start menu, type cmd, and hit Enter.Inside the VM, run:DOSipconfig
Look at the IPv4 address. Did it actually get 192.168.56.10, or did it get a weird 169.254.x.x (APIPA) address?Step 3: The "Vagrant Reload" Fix90% of the time, this is caused by a race condition during the very first boot. If the VM didn't get the right IP, or if the network adapter hung, we just need to tell Vagrant to re-apply the network settings.Close the VMware Workstation GUI (let it run in the background).Open an Administrator Command Prompt in Windows.Navigate back to your provider folder:DOScd C:\Users\hs32\Desktop\GOAD\workspace\57aa65-goad-vmware\provider
Run the reload command:DOSvagrant reload
This command safely reboots all 5 VMs and explicitly forces VMware to re-map the network adapters and static IPs.Run those quick checks (ipconfig on your host, ipconfig in the VM) and let me know what you see! We are inches away from the finish line.

Vagrant asked VMware to build a bridge to the 192.168.56.x subnet, VMware created VMnet2 to do it, but Windows threw its hands up and assigned a dead-end IP address instead of 192.168.56.1.Because your host machine doesn't have an IP on the 192.168.56.x subnet, it drops all traffic meant for the VMs.Here is how to manually force VMware and Windows to fix that virtual switch:Step 1: Fix the VMware Virtual Network EditorWe need to hardcode the correct subnet into VMware so Windows respects it.Open your Windows Start Menu, type Virtual Network Editor, and open it.At the bottom right of the window, click the button that says Change Settings (this will prompt you for Administrator privileges and unlock the grayed-out options).In the list of networks at the top, click on VMnet2.Ensure the Host-only radio button is selected in the middle section.At the very bottom, change the Subnet IP to 192.168.56.0.Ensure the Subnet mask is 255.255.255.0.Click Apply, wait a few seconds for it to restart the virtual network services, and then click OK.Step 2: Restart the Lab (Vagrant Reload)Now that the physical bridge exists, we need to quickly bounce the virtual machines so they attach to the newly repaired network switch.Go back to your Windows Command Prompt.Ensure you are in your deployment directory:

I hear you, and I know this is the absolute most infuriating part of setting up a virtual lab on Windows. If you let it run without touching it and it is still hitting a brick wall at the DHCP check, we are going to stop playing by Vagrant's rules.Vagrant is blind. We are going to bypass Vagrant's automation, go inside the machine, and force the connection ourselves.Leave your command prompt running exactly where it is (stuck at "Waiting for the VM to receive an address..."). Do not hit Ctrl+C.Here is how we hack the boot sequence to force it through:Step 1: The "Inside the Box" OverrideWe are going to log into the VM and manually kick the network card to wake it up.Open your VMware Workstation GUI.Click on GOAD-DC01 and look at the console. It should be sitting at the Windows Ctrl + Alt + Delete lock screen.Click inside the window (press Ctrl + Alt + Insert on your keyboard to send the unlock command).Log in with these credentials:Username: vagrantPassword: vagrantOnce you are on the desktop, click the Windows Start button, type cmd, and hit Enter to open the Command Prompt inside the VM.Type this exact command and hit Enter:DOSipconfig /renew
(Watch your Vagrant terminal on your host machine. Often, just running this command forces the VM to grab the IP, Vagrant instantly detects it, and the script continues!)Step 2: The "Vagrant Utility" Bug (If Step 1 fails)If ipconfig /renew doesn't instantly unblock Vagrant, or if the VM tells you it already has a 192.168.56.x IP address, you have hit a known bug. There is a hidden background service on your host computer that acts as the translator between VMware and Vagrant. If it crashes, Vagrant goes deaf.On your physical Windows host (not the VM), press the Windows Key, type Services, and hit Enter.Scroll all the way down to the V's and find Vagrant VMware Utility.Right-click it and select Restart (or Start if it is stopped).Next, find VMware DHCP Service and VMware NAT Service in that same list and right-click -> Restart both of them.Step 3: The Hardcoded BypassIf the services are running and the VM still refuses to pull a DHCP address, we will manually hardcode the IP address inside the VM so Vagrant finally sees it.Inside your GOAD-DC01 VM desktop, open PowerShell as an Administrator.Run this command to force the exact IP address Vagrant is waiting for:PowerShellNew-NetIPAddress -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet0" -IPAddress "192.168.56.10" -PrefixLength 24 -DefaultGateway "192.168.56.1"
(Note: If your network adapter is named something like "Ethernet1", change the InterfaceAlias to match).The millisecond that VM binds to 192.168.56.10, Vagrant should detect it on the host side, print Fixed port collision..., and finally move on to building DC02.Let me know what the VM screen actually shows right now!

i want to change the host vm and full setup  should i go for linux host or windows

### Assistant

If you have the hardware flexibility to switch, go with a Linux host 100%. Honestly, after the absolute nightmare you just endured with VMware’s registry locks, APIPA IP addresses, and background service freezes, you have experienced exactly why the cybersecurity community deeply dislikes hosting complex labs on Windows.Given your technical background, moving this setup to a native Linux environment will feel like a breath of fresh air. Here is a candid breakdown of why Linux is the gold standard for deploying environments like GOAD, and why Windows fights you every step of the way.Why Linux is the Ultimate Lab HostNative Ansible (No WSL Gymnastics): On Windows, you have to run Vagrant in PowerShell, but Ansible in Ubuntu (WSL), and hope the network bridge between the two doesn't collapse. On Linux, Vagrant and Ansible run in the exact same native terminal. No bridging, no translation, no file path headaches.Bulletproof Networking (KVM/libvirt): Instead of fighting VMware or VirtualBox, you can use KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine) with libvirt on Linux. The network switches are managed directly by the Linux kernel. They don't freeze, they don't lock files, and they don't randomly drop DHCP leases.Massively Reduced Overhead: Windows 10/11 consumes a massive amount of RAM and CPU just to exist. Linux is incredibly lean, meaning you can dedicate far more of your system's resources to the actual Active Directory VMs, making the lab run much faster.Total System Control: If a network interface gets stuck on Linux, you can instantly kill it and rebuild it via the command line. You don't have to restart your whole computer just to unlock a file.The Case for Sticking with WindowsThere is really only one reason to stick with Windows: If this is your only computer and you need it for daily driving. If you rely on Windows-exclusive software, PC gaming, or don't want to deal with dual-booting, you are stuck with the Windows/VMware/WSL stack. It can work (as you were extremely close to doing!), but it requires patience and a willingness to occasionally nuke the virtual networks from orbit.The VerdictIf you are comfortable configuring a Linux system (whether that is Ubuntu, Debian, or even a rolling release like Arch if you want maximum control), ditching Windows for this project is the best decision you can make. Deploying GOAD using vagrant-libvirt on Linux is a fast, streamlined, and highly stable process.If you are ready to burn the Windows setup down, what kind of Linux deployment are you thinking about—wiping this machine entirely, setting up a dual-boot, or moving to a dedicated secondary rig?

is it better to have host linux vm to have gui or without

### Assistant

This is a fantastic architectural question, especially since you are building a heavy, resource-intensive lab like GOAD.The choice between a GUI (Desktop) and Headless (Command Line Only) Linux host completely changes how you interact with your lab. Here is the candid breakdown of both approaches for your specific use case.Option 1: Headless Linux (No GUI)This is the traditional "Server" approach. You install something like Ubuntu Server or Debian, plug it into the wall, and connect to it remotely via SSH from your laptop.The Pros:Maximum Performance: A headless Linux server uses almost zero resources (often under 500MB of RAM). Every single drop of your CPU and memory goes directly to your GOAD virtual machines.Rock Solid: No desktop environments (like GNOME or KDE) to freeze, crash, or consume background processing power.Forces Good Habits: You manage everything via virsh (the KVM command line) and Ansible, which makes you incredibly fast at terminal operations.The Cons:No Visual Troubleshooting: If a VM's network gets stuck (like we just saw on Windows), you can't just open a console window to look at the Windows boot screen.Tooling Disconnect: You have to run your attack tools (like BloodHound, Burp Suite, or a web browser) on a separate attacking machine and route the traffic in.Option 2: Linux with a GUI (Desktop)This is the "Workstation" approach. You install Ubuntu Desktop, Pop!_OS, or Fedora, and use it just like you were using Windows.The Pros:Visual VM Management: You get to use Virtual Machine Manager (virt-manager). It is a fantastic, native Linux GUI for KVM that lets you see your virtual networks, easily configure hardware, and pop open console screens to see what the VMs are doing.All-in-One Hacking Station: You can run your Kali Linux VM, BloodHound, web browsers, and code editors directly on the host machine alongside GOAD.Easier Transition: Moving from Windows to a Linux Desktop is much less jarring than moving straight to a headless terminal.The Cons:Resource Tax: Modern Linux GUIs (like GNOME) will consume about 1.5GB to 2GB of RAM just to render the desktop. If you are tight on RAM, that is memory stolen from GOAD.The Verdict for a Pentesting LabUnless you are installing this on a dedicated server box sitting in a closet, I highly recommend installing Linux WITH a GUI for this project.Having access to virt-manager is an absolute lifesaver when troubleshooting Active Directory setups, and having a local browser to quickly research exploits or view web interfaces inside the lab network is incredibly convenient. If you are worried about the RAM tax, you can install a lightweight flavor of Linux (like Xubuntu or Linux Mint XFCE) which gives you a GUI for less than 1GB of memory overhead.To help narrow down the exact distribution and setup, what does the hardware look like on the machine you plan to use for this (specifically CPU cores and total RAM)?

so at my fresh ubuntu.. how do i set all prerequisites of goad

Welcome to the Linux side! You are going to immediately notice how much faster and more transparent this process is compared to fighting Windows registries.Since you are on a fresh Ubuntu install with a GUI, we are going to build the ultimate, native KVM/libvirt environment. This completely bypasses the need for VMware or VirtualBox, tapping directly into the Linux kernel for maximum performance and stable networking.Here is your exact, copy-paste guide to setting up the prerequisites for GOAD.Phase 1: The Native Hypervisor (KVM & virt-manager)First, we will install the Linux kernel virtual machine tools and the GUI (virt-manager) so you can actually see your VMs booting up.Open your Ubuntu terminal (Ctrl + Alt + T).Update your fresh system and install the KVM stack:Bashsudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y qemu-kvm libvirt-daemon-system libvirt-clients bridge-utils virt-manager
Critical Step: Add your current user to the virtualization groups so you don't have to run everything as the root user.Bashsudo usermod -aG libvirt $USER
sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER
Phase 2: Vagrant & The HashiCorp RepoUbuntu's default software store has an outdated version of Vagrant. We need the official, latest version directly from HashiCorp.Add the HashiCorp security key and repository:Bashwget -O- https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg] https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com $(lsb_release -cs) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/hashicorp.list
Install Vagrant:Bashsudo apt update && sudo apt install -y vagrant
Phase 3: The vagrant-libvirt PluginThis is the magic bridge that allows Vagrant to talk to the Linux kernel instead of VirtualBox. It requires a few development libraries to compile correctly.Install the compile dependencies:Bashsudo apt install -y ruby-dev libvirt-dev build-essential
Install the plugin:Bashvagrant plugin install vagrant-libvirt
Phase 4: Python & GitFinally, we need the standard Linux tools to clone the GOAD repository and run its Python orchestrator.Install Python virtual environments and Git:Bashsudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv git
Phase 5: The Reboot (Do Not Skip!)Because we added your user to the libvirt and kvm security groups in Phase 1, you must reboot your computer for Ubuntu to apply those permissions.Bashsudo reboot
Next Steps Once You Reboot...When you log back in, your system is fully prepped. You can clone the repo and set up your Python environment just like you are used to:Bashgit clone https://github.com/Orange-Cyberdefense/GOAD.git
cd GOAD
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.yml
When you are ready to generate the config files, you will simply swap out the provider flag to use libvirt:Bashpython3 goad.py -t install -l GOAD -p libvirt

### Assistant

You are incredibly close. The Python orchestrator worked perfectly, Vagrant successfully talked to libvirt, and it even downloaded the 40GB Windows Server images for you!But right at the exact millisecond it tried to turn the VMs on, it crashed with this error:
invalid argument: could not get preferred machine for /usr/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 type=kvmI looked closely at your command prompt, and I see this: hs32@thesisvm.This tells me exactly what is happening: You are running this Ubuntu Linux setup inside a Virtual Machine (likely on your Windows host), rather than installed directly on your physical hardware.The Problem: Virtualization InceptionKVM requires direct access to your physical CPU's hardware virtualization chips (Intel VT-x or AMD-V). Because your Ubuntu machine is already a virtual machine, it thinks it doesn't have physical CPU access. When Vagrant asks Ubuntu to build the GOAD VMs, QEMU/KVM panics because it cannot run a Virtual Machine inside another Virtual Machine by default.The Fix: Enable Nested VirtualizationYou don't need to rebuild anything, you just need to pass the CPU's hardware acceleration through your host hypervisor into your Ubuntu VM.Step 1: Power Off the Ubuntu VMRun this in your Ubuntu terminal to shut it down completely:Bashsudo shutdown now
Step 2: Flip the Switch in your Host HypervisorGo back to your physical Windows machine. How you do this depends on what you are using to run your thesisvm:If using VMware Workstation: Right-click the Ubuntu VM -> Settings -> Click on Processors -> Check the box for "Virtualize Intel VT-x/EPT or AMD-V/RVI". Click OK.If using VirtualBox: Right-click the Ubuntu VM -> Settings -> System -> Processor tab -> Check the box for "Enable Nested VT-x/AMD-V".(Note: If you actually installed Ubuntu natively on the bare metal of your computer and aren't in a VM, this means hardware virtualization is disabled in your computer's BIOS, and you need to restart your PC and enable it there).Step 3: Verify it WorksPower your Ubuntu VM back on, open a terminal, and check if KVM can now see your CPU:Bashsudo apt install cpu-checker
kvm-ok
If it says "KVM acceleration can be used", you are golden!Step 4: Resume the BuildBecause the last build crashed halfway through, Vagrant left some broken pieces behind. We need to clear them out before we try again.Navigate back to the provider folder and clean it up:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/4da4be-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant destroy -f
Finally, fire the build one more time:Bashvagrant up
Now that KVM has hardware access, it will fly through domain creation! Let it run!

### Assistant

That is a massive pivot, but honestly, moving to a dedicated cloud instance is a fantastic architectural decision. You just bypassed all local hardware limitations, and Azure's backend network speeds will pull those 40GB Vagrant boxes down in minutes.However, moving to Azure introduces a brand new, enterprise-level plot twist to the exact error you just hit (could not get preferred machine... type=kvm).Because Azure VMs are themselves virtual machines, you are still dealing with Nested Virtualization. Azure does support nested KVM, but Microsoft explicitly blocks hardware virtualization on 90% of their VM sizes. If you spun up a basic standard instance (like a B-series or an A-series), KVM will not work. Here is exactly how to verify your Azure setup and configure it for a headless GOAD deployment.Step 1: The Azure VM Size CheckTo run KVM inside Azure, your VM must be one of the specific families that supports nested virtualization. Typically, these are the v3, v4, or v5 series (e.g., Standard_D8s_v3 or Standard_E4s_v4).Furthermore, GOAD is heavy. You need an instance with at least 4 vCPUs (8 is highly recommended) and an absolute minimum of 16GB of RAM (32GB recommended).Run this command in your Azure Ubuntu terminal right now to see if your CPU is passing the VT-x flags through:Bashsudo apt update && sudo apt install -y cpu-checker
kvm-ok
If it says KVM acceleration can be used: You picked the right VM size!If it fails: You need to log into the Azure Portal, stop the VM, and click Size. Resize the VM to something like a Standard_D8s_v3 or Standard_D4s_v3, start it back up, and kvm-ok will magically pass.Step 2: The Headless SetupSince this is an Azure server, you don't have a GUI or virt-manager by default. You are operating entirely in a headless terminal.The prerequisites we covered earlier still apply perfectly. Run this to install the headless KVM and Vagrant stack:Bashsudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y qemu-kvm libvirt-daemon-system libvirt-clients bridge-utils python3 python3-pip python3-venv git

sudo usermod -aG libvirt $USER
sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER
Install HashiCorp Vagrant:Bashwget -O- https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg] https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com $(lsb_release -cs) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/hashicorp.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y vagrant
Install the Libvirt Plugin (requires build tools):Bashsudo apt install -y ruby-dev libvirt-dev build-essential
vagrant plugin install vagrant-libvirt
Reboot your Azure VM so the user group permissions apply:Bashsudo reboot
Step 3: Deploying GOAD (The Libvirt Branch)Once your SSH session reconnects, pull the specific GOAD branch that supports Libvirt, just like before:Bashgit clone https://github.com/Orange-Cyberdefense/GOAD.git
cd GOAD
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.yml

git fetch origin pull/475/head:libvirt-support
git checkout libvirt-support
Now, generate the configuration and build it:Bashpython3 goad.py -t install -l GOAD -p libvirt
# Note the folder name it generates
cd workspace/<YOUR-NEW-FOLDER-NAME>/provider
vagrant up
Because Azure's hypervisor is heavily optimized, this deployment will run significantly smoother than local desktop virtualization, provided KVM has access to the CPU.Since this lab will be generating a private 192.168.56.x subnet deep inside Azure, how are you planning to route your attacking tools into that cloud environment—are you going to set up an OpenVPN/Wireguard tunnel, or just spin up a Kali VM inside that same Azure virtual network?

### Assistant

Got it. My apologies for the confusion! Since you are running this entirely on an Ubuntu machine hosted in Azure, the hypervisor choice makes total sense now. And to answer your previous question: KVM/libvirt is still absolutely the right choice over VMware or VirtualBox for an Azure Linux host.However, you are hitting the exact final boss of cloud-hosted labs.The error could not get preferred machine for /usr/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 type=kvm happens when Vagrant tries to request hardware virtualization from the Azure server, but Microsoft's hypervisor says, "No, you aren't allowed to do that."By default, Azure blocks virtual machines from running their own virtual machines (Nested Virtualization). It completely disables the KVM hardware chips on the CPU.Here is exactly how to fix it directly in Azure.Step 1: Verify the BlockRun this command in your Azure Ubuntu terminal right now:Bashsudo kvm-ok
It is almost certainly going to output: INFO: Your CPU does not support KVM extensions. This proves Azure is currently blocking it.Step 2: Change Your Azure VM SizeAzure does support nested virtualization, but only on specific VM sizes (specifically the v3, v4, and v5 families). If you deployed a standard B-series (Burstable) or a v2 instance, it will never work.Log into your Azure Portal in your web browser.Go to your thesisvm virtual machine.Click on Stop to deallocate the VM.On the left menu, click Size.You must select a VM size that ends in v3, v4, or v5.Recommendation: GOAD is extremely heavy. You need at least 4 vCPUs and 16GB of RAM. Look for Standard_D4s_v3 (bare minimum) or Standard_D8s_v3 (recommended for smooth performance).Click Resize.Once it resizes, click Start to boot the VM back up.Step 3: Verify the FixSSH back into your Ubuntu terminal and run the check again:Bashsudo kvm-ok
It should now say: INFO: /dev/kvm exists. KVM acceleration can be used.Step 4: Clean Up and RebuildBecause your last run crashed exactly at the moment it tried to build the hard drives, Vagrant left broken, half-created files behind. We must delete them before trying again.Navigate back into your provider directory:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/4da4be-goad-libvirt/provider
Destroy the broken state forcefully:Bashvagrant destroy -f
Boot the lab:Bashvagrant up
Because your Azure VM now officially has hardware virtualization enabled, KVM will instantly map the CPUs, bypass that error, and begin turning on the domain controllers!

## Turn 54

### User

Standard E4as v4 (4 vcpus, 32 GiB memory)  i am already using this

### Assistant

You are hitting a very specific, often overlooked Azure naming trap.The problem is the single letter "a" in your instance name (Standard_E4as_v4).In Azure's naming convention, the "a" stands for AMD. While Microsoft does support nested virtualization on their v3 and v4 series VMs, they only support it on the Intel processors for those specific generations. The AMD v4 instances (Eas_v4 and Das_v4) physically have KVM blocked at the host hypervisor level.Here is the exact path to fix it.Step 1: Change to an Intel VM SizeYou need to resize the VM to drop the AMD processor.Go to the Azure Portal and Stop your VM.Click on Size in the left menu.Select an Intel equivalent. Good options include:Standard_E4s_v4 (Notice there is no 'a')Standard_E4s_v3Standard_D8s_v3 (A highly recommended 8-core Intel size for running GOAD smoothly)Click Resize and start the VM.Step 2: The "Trusted Launch" Trap (Critical Check)There is a second roadblock you need to verify before booting up. Azure now defaults all new VMs to a security setting called Trusted Launch.Trusted Launch completely disables nested virtualization, even on supported Intel CPUs.In the Azure Portal, look at your VM's Overview page and find the Security Type field.If it says Standard, you are good to go just by resizing.If it says Trusted Launch, resizing the CPU will not fix the KVM error. Azure does not let you downgrade security types on the fly. You will have to completely delete this Azure VM and recreate a new one, ensuring you manually select Standard under the Security Type dropdown on the very first page of the creation wizard.Step 3: Verify and BuildOnce you are on an Intel CPU with Standard security, SSH back into your Ubuntu terminal and run the hardware check:Bashsudo kvm-ok
As soon as that outputs INFO: /dev/kvm exists. KVM acceleration can be used, your environment is fully unlocked.Clean out the broken Vagrant state from the last attempt:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/4da4be-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant destroy -f
Finally, fire the build command:Bashvagrant up
With the hardware unlocked, Vagrant will immediately bypass that error and start turning on the virtual networks!

i am at Standard E4s v3  but from the vm pageat azure.. i get that.. at screenshot

### Assistant

That screenshot is the smoking gun. You successfully fixed the CPU issue by moving to the Standard_E4s_v3 Intel instance, but you have officially hit the Trusted Launch trap.As you can see in your screenshot, the Security type is set to Trusted launch.Trusted Launch is a great feature for enterprise servers, but it fundamentally breaks lab environments. It locks down the hypervisor, enforces Secure Boot, and strictly forbids nested virtualization (KVM)—even if the physical Intel CPU supports it.Here is the frustrating reality of Azure: You cannot downgrade a VM from Trusted Launch to Standard after it has been created. The dropdown to change it is permanently greyed out.To get GOAD running, you have to do a quick rebuild.The Fix: Deploy with Standard SecuritySince you haven't actually been able to build the lab inside this Ubuntu VM yet, destroying it and spinning up a new one will only take a few minutes.Delete the VM: Go to the Azure Portal, select this thesisvm, and delete it (make sure to check the box to delete the associated OS disk and public IP so you aren't charged for ghost resources).Create a New VM: Start the standard Azure VM creation process.The Critical Setting: On the very first tab (Basics), scroll down just past the Region selector. You will see a dropdown called Security type.Change it from "Trusted launch virtual machines" to Standard.Select Size: Pick your Standard_E4s_v3 or Standard_D8s_v3 size.Finish creating the VM as usual.Once you SSH into this new "Standard" security VM and run your prerequisite install script, kvm-ok will finally pass, and Vagrant will spin up those Active Directory boxes without breaking a sweat!

### Assistant

🏆 Massive Victory Achieved!Look closely at your logs right before the crash:GOAD-DC03: WinRM address: 192.168.121.61:5986
GOAD-DC01: WinRM address: 192.168.121.215:5986KVM is working perfectly. Your Azure nested virtualization block is officially bypassed. Vagrant successfully talked to the Linux kernel, created the virtual switches, built the virtual machines, booted them, and successfully handed them IP addresses!Why it Failed: The 4-Core Traffic JamIt crashed with a "Timed out while waiting for the machine to boot" error because of a hardware bottleneck.You are running a Standard_E4s_v3 instance, which has 4 vCPUs. GOAD's default configuration tries to boot all 5 Windows Server VMs simultaneously. Since each VM is configured to use 2 CPUs, you just asked 4 physical cores to do the work of 10 cores simultaneously while Windows was running its heavy first-time setup (Sysprep).The CPU queuing was so severe that Windows took longer than Vagrant's default 10-minute timeout to turn on its Remote Management (WinRM) service. Vagrant simply got impatient and quit.The Fix: Boot SequentiallyWe need to tell Vagrant to boot these machines one at a time. This allows your 4 Azure cores to focus entirely on getting one Windows machine fully booted and stable before moving on to the next.Here is exactly how to do it:Step 1: Clean Up the Locked StateBecause Vagrant panicked, it locked GOAD-DC02 and left the others in a half-configured state. Wipe the slate clean so we can do a proper sequential boot.Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/3905e4-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant destroy -f
Step 2: The Sequential Boot CommandRun the build command again, but this time, add the flag to disable parallel provisioning.Bashvagrant up --no-parallel
What to Expect NowBecause the heavy 40GB Windows boxes are already downloaded and cached in libvirt, it will immediately start building.It will boot GOAD-DC01, wait for it to fully come online and respond to WinRM, apply the initial network configurations, and only then move on to GOAD-DC02. This is going to take a bit of time (roughly 20-30 minutes total), but it will not time out this time! Let it run!

### Assistant

This is the classic "Nested Virtualization Penalty."Even though you restricted Vagrant to building one machine at a time, you are running a virtualized Windows Server inside a virtualized Linux server. Because of that double-layer of virtualization, Windows is running its initial, heavy setup (Sysprep) incredibly slowly.Vagrant has a hardcoded default patience limit (usually 10 minutes). Windows actually booted fine, grabbed its IP address (192.168.121.239), and started configuring itself, but because it took longer than 10 minutes to turn on WinRM, Vagrant panicked, assumed it crashed, and auto-deleted the VM (Removing domain...).We need to tell Vagrant to sit down, wait, and give Windows the 30+ minutes it actually needs to finish installing itself.The Fix: Increase the Boot TimeoutYou need to manually edit the Vagrantfile that the Python script generated to increase the timeout window.Step 1: Open the Configuration File
Make sure you are in the provider directory, and open the file with the nano text editor:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/3905e4-goad-libvirt/provider
nano Vagrantfile
Step 2: Inject the Timeout Command
Look at the very top of the file for the line that says Vagrant.configure("2") do |config|.
Immediately below that line, add this exact command to extend the timeout to 40 minutes (2400 seconds):RubyVagrant.configure("2") do |config|
  config.vm.boot_timeout = 2400
Step 3: Save and ExitPress Ctrl + O (the letter O, not zero) to save the file.Press Enter to confirm the file name.Press Ctrl + X to exit the editor.Step 4: The Final Build
Now, fire off the build command exactly like you did before. Because you previously destroyed the broken state, it will start completely fresh.Bashvagrant up --no-parallel
Walk away and grab a coffee. Vagrant will now patiently wait up to 40 minutes per machine for Windows to finish building its registry, generating its encryption keys, and turning on WinRM. It will slowly but surely march through all 5 machines!

### Assistant

This is actually massive progress! Look at your logs: DC01, DC02, and DC03 all successfully built, booted, and configured themselves perfectly! You are currently sitting with 3 fully functional Windows Server Active Directory instances running on your Azure host.Why SRV02 Failed (The CPU Traffic Jam)The timeout happened on GOAD-SRV02 because of simple resource starvation.
Your Azure host (Standard_E4s_v3) has 4 CPU cores. Right now, DC01, DC02, and DC03 are all powered on and actively running in the background. When Vagrant tried to build SRV02, it had to fight the other three servers for CPU cycles. Because it was starved for processing power, the Windows installation crawled to a halt and missed the timeout window.The Fix: The "Pause and Build" StrategyThe brilliant thing about Vagrant is that it remembers state. We don't need to rebuild the first three machines. We just need to temporarily turn them off to free up your CPU, let SRV02 and SRV03 use 100% of the host's power to build, and then turn everything back on.Here is the exact sequence to get past the finish line:Step 1: Shut Down the Domain ControllersRun this command to gracefully power off the three machines that are currently hogging your CPU:Bashvagrant halt GOAD-DC01 GOAD-DC02 GOAD-DC03
Step 2: Build the ServersNow that your host CPU is completely freed up, tell Vagrant to exclusively build the remaining two machines sequentially:Bashvagrant up GOAD-SRV02 GOAD-SRV03 --no-parallel
(Because they have all 4 cores to themselves, they will boot up much faster and successfully pass the WinRM check!)Step 3: Turn Everything Back OnOnce SRV02 and SRV03 successfully finish building and return you to the command prompt, simply run:Bashvagrant up
(Turning a VM on takes drastically less CPU than installing it from scratch. Vagrant will quickly power on DC01, DC02, and DC03 without hitting any timeouts).Once that final command finishes, your entire 5-machine infrastructure is fully built and ready for the Ansible provisioning phase!

You now have a pristine, high-performance foundation running in the cloud.The Final Phase: Ansible ProvisioningRight now, these are just 5 blank Windows Server machines. They don't know they are supposed to be a vulnerable Active Directory forest yet.We are going to use Ansible to reach into those machines and install Active Directory, create the domains (like sevenkingdoms.local), generate all the vulnerable users, and configure the specific security flaws that make GOAD the ultimate pentesting lab.Here is the exact sequence to trigger the final build.Step 1: Navigate to the Ansible DirectoryMove out of your Vagrant provider folder and into the main Ansible directory:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible

Let it run completely uninterrupted until it drops you back at the command prompt with a final "Play Recap" showing the successful tasks.Once the playbook finishes and the lab is officially alive, which domain or vulnerability path are you planning to attack first?

### Assistant

This is an incredibly frustrating error right at the finish line, but the good news is that this has absolutely nothing to do with your Azure setup or your virtual machines. You just ran headfirst into a well-known Python compatibility bug.The Problem: Python 3.12 vs. Old AnsibleIf you look closely at your traceback, you can see you are running Python 3.12 (/home/hs32/Desktop/GOAD/.venv/lib/python3.12/...).When you originally ran the pip install -r requirements.yml command earlier today, GOAD specifically downloaded an older, pinned version of Ansible (specifically ansible-core 2.12.6).Python 3.12 completely removed a legacy background tool used for finding modules (the find_module hook), replacing it with a new one (find_spec). Because ansible-core 2.12 is older, it doesn't know what find_spec is, so the second it tries to wake up, it crashes.The Fix: Force-Upgrade AnsibleWe just need to force your Python virtual environment to install a modern version of Ansible that knows how to talk to Python 3.12.Step 1: Upgrade ansible-core
Make sure your virtual environment is still activated (you should see (.venv) at the start of your prompt), and run this:Bashpip install --upgrade ansible-core
(This will bump Ansible up to version 2.15 or newer, which perfectly supports Python 3.12).Step 2: Re-run the Playbook
Once the upgrade finishes, just fire the exact same command you just tried:Bashansible-playbook -i ../workspace/3905e4-goad-libvirt/inventory main.yml
Because your VMs are already perfectly booted and waiting, Ansible will immediately start connecting to them over WinRM and begin the massive Active Directory configuration sequence. You are moments away from the green text!

You hit a classic "missing variables" trap!If you look closely at the very first error at the top of your log:
skipping vars_files item due to an undefined variable
"{{data_path}}/config.json"Ansible is complaining because it doesn't know which lab data to use. GOAD is modular—it can build the full "GOAD" lab, or smaller labs like "sccm" or "vulnerable-ad". Because we just ran the raw ansible-playbook command, we didn't pass it the specific configuration files for the GOAD layout, so it skipped every single machine because it didn't know what to do with them!The good news? The fix is incredibly easy. We are going to let the Python orchestrator do the heavy lifting, just like it did for the VM creation. It will automatically inject all those missing variables and fire off Ansible for you.The Fix: Use the GOAD OrchestratorStep 1: Move back to the main directory
Get out of the ansible folder and go back to where the goad.py script lives:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD
Step 2: Run the Provisioning Command

This is an excellent idea. You just survived an absolute masterclass in infrastructure engineering, cloud architecture, and automation troubleshooting. When you are building enterprise-level labs like GOAD, documenting the roadblocks is just as important as the final result.Here are your official "Battle Notes" for how you conquered the GOAD Azure deployment. Save these for the next time you (or a teammate) need to build this from scratch.🏆 GOAD Deployment Post-Mortem & Cheat SheetPhase 1: Cloud Architecture & The Nested KVM TrapsThe Goal: Run KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine) inside an Ubuntu server hosted on Azure.
The Challenge: Azure heavily restricts VMs from running their own VMs (Nested Virtualization).Trap 1: The AMD Block. We initially deployed an E4as_v4 instance. The "a" stands for AMD. Azure physically blocks nested virtualization on their AMD host servers.The Fix: Switched to an Intel-based instance (Standard_E4s_v3).Trap 2: The Trusted Launch Lockout. Modern Azure defaults to "Trusted Launch" security, which strictly forbids hardware virtualization for security reasons, even on compatible Intel CPUs.The Fix: Deleted the VM and recreated it, ensuring the Security type was explicitly set to Standard on the first page of the creation wizard.Verification: Running sudo kvm-ok finally returned KVM acceleration can be used.Phase 2: The Vagrant Build & The CPU Traffic JamThe Goal: Use Vagrant to download and boot 5 heavy Windows Server virtual machines simultaneously.
The Challenge: Vagrant kept timing out and auto-deleting the VMs right as they were finishing their Windows setup.The Root Cause: We were running a 4-core Azure VM. Vagrant tried to boot all 5 Windows machines at the exact same time. The CPU queuing was so severe that Windows couldn't finish its Sysprep and turn on WinRM before Vagrant's default 10-minute patience ran out.The Fixes:Stop the Stampede: We passed the --no-parallel flag to force Vagrant to build one machine at a time, dedicating all 4 host cores to a single Windows installation.Increase Patience: We edited the generated Vagrantfile and injected config.vm.boot_timeout = 2400 (40 minutes) to give the double-virtualized Windows OS enough time to build its registry and keys.Phase 3: Ansible & The Python BugThe Goal: Run the Ansible playbook to automatically configure the blank Windows machines into a vulnerable Active Directory forest.
The Challenge: Ansible crashed three different times for three completely different reasons.Crash 1: Python 3.12 vs Legacy Ansible. GOAD's requirements file downloaded an old version of ansible-core (2.12). Python 3.12 removed the legacy find_module code that old Ansible relied on, causing an immediate fatal crash.The Fix: Upgraded Ansible to a modern version inside the virtual environment: pip install --upgrade ansible-core.Crash 2: Missing Tools. Ansible complained it couldn't find the win_dns_client module. The core installation was too lightweight and lacked Windows support.The Fix: Downloaded the required external collections using ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml.Crash 3: The Missing Variables & Syntax. Running the raw ansible-playbook command failed because it didn't know which lab configuration data to use. Moving to the GOAD interactive console fixed the variables, but it failed when we just typed provision main.The Fix: The Python orchestrator needs the exact file extension. Running provision main.yml in the interactive console perfectly injected the variables and launched the script.📝 Next Steps: What to do when Ansible FinishesOnce that massive wall of green text finishes and drops you back at the command prompt, your lab is live. Here is what you should do immediately:Take a Snapshot (Crucial):
Because you are running on libvirt, you should snapshot the pristine, vulnerable state of the lab before you start attacking it. If you break the domain during a pentest, you can just revert the snapshot instead of spending hours rebuilding.Bashvagrant snapshot save pristine-goad
Verify Connectivity:
Ensure your host machine can talk to the new domain.Bashping 192.168.56.10   # Pings the primary Domain Controller (GOAD-DC01)
Start Attacking:
You now have the sevenkingdoms.local and essos.local domains fully functional. You can start routing your tools (like CrackMapExec, BloodHound, or Impacket) at the 192.168.56.X subnet right from your Azure Ubuntu host, or set up a VPN tunnel to access it from your local machine.

### Assistant

Here is the complete, comprehensive cheat sheet, updated to include every single command, sequence, and configuration tweak you executed to get this lab running.🏆 The Complete GOAD on Azure libvirt Playbook1. The Azure VM Hardware RequirementsSize: Must be an Intel CPU (e.g., Standard_E4s_v3 or Standard_D8s_v3). Avoid AMD (a in the name like E4as) because Azure blocks KVM on them.Security Type: Must be set to Standard during the initial VM creation. If it is set to "Trusted Launch", nested virtualization is permanently blocked.Verification Command:Bashsudo kvm-ok
# MUST return: "KVM acceleration can be used"

#### 2. Base System Prerequisites
```bash
# Install KVM, Python, and Git
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y qemu-kvm libvirt-daemon-system libvirt-clients bridge-utils python3 python3-pip python3-venv git cpu-checker

# Add user to virtualization groups (Requires Reboot after)
sudo usermod -aG libvirt $USER
sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER

# Install HashiCorp Vagrant
wget -O- https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg] https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com $(lsb_release -cs) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/hashicorp.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y vagrant

# Install vagrant-libvirt plugin
sudo apt install -y ruby-dev libvirt-dev build-essential
vagrant plugin install vagrant-libvirt

# Reboot to apply group permissions
sudo reboot
3. Fetching GOAD & The Libvirt BranchBashgit clone https://github.com/Orange-Cyberdefense/GOAD.git
cd GOAD

# Setup Python Virtual Environment
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.yml

# Fetch the specific Libvirt pull request branch
git fetch origin pull/475/head:libvirt-support
git checkout libvirt-support
4. Generating the Lab & Fixing Vagrant TimeoutsBecause the Azure VM only has 4 vCPUs, booting 5 Windows Server VMs simultaneously causes CPU starvation, leading to WinRM timeouts.Bash# Generate the lab files
python3 goad.py -t install -l GOAD -p libvirt

# Navigate to the generated provider directory (replace 3905e4 with your unique ID)
cd workspace/3905e4-goad-libvirt/provider

# Inject the 40-minute boot timeout into Vagrantfile
nano Vagrantfile
# ADD THIS LINE under Vagrant.configure("2") do |config|:
# config.vm.boot_timeout = 2400

# Clear out any broken states
vagrant destroy -f

# Boot the first three Domain Controllers sequentially
vagrant up GOAD-DC01 GOAD-DC02 GOAD-DC03 --no-parallel

# Pause them to free up the host CPU
vagrant halt GOAD-DC01 GOAD-DC02 GOAD-DC03

# Boot the remaining two servers sequentially
vagrant up GOAD-SRV02 GOAD-SRV03 --no-parallel

# Power the Domain Controllers back on (fast boot)
vagrant up
5. Ansible Configuration & Bug FixesThe default GOAD requirements pull an older version of Ansible that breaks on Python 3.12, and it lacks the necessary Windows modules.Bash# Navigate to the Ansible directory
cd ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible

# Fix Python 3.12 compatibility bug by forcing an Ansible upgrade
pip install --upgrade ansible-core

# Install the missing Windows and AD modules
ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml
6. Launching the ProvisionerRunning the raw ansible-playbook command fails because it lacks the necessary config.json lab variables. The interactive console bypasses this entirely.Bash# Navigate back to the GOAD root
cd ~/Desktop/GOAD

# Launch the interactive console
python3 goad.py

# Inside the GOAD > prompt, inject the main playbook to start configuring AD
provision main.yml

### Assistant

Bringing this lab home to your local machine is a brilliant move. Running GOAD natively on bare-metal hardware completely eliminates the nested virtualization traps, Trusted Launch lockouts, and CPU starvation issues you were fighting in Azure.Because you are running Arch Linux, you have a massive advantage: the official pacman repositories maintain incredibly up-to-date versions of KVM, Vagrant, and Ansible, which makes dodging those Python 3.12 compatibility bugs much easier.Here is your end-to-end battle plan for standing up GOAD natively on Arch.Phase 1: The Arch Native KVM StackArch doesn't enable services by default, so we need to install the hypervisor tools and manually turn on the libvirt network daemon.Install the full virtualization stack from the official repos:Bashsudo pacman -Syu
sudo pacman -S qemu-full libvirt virt-manager dnsmasq iptables-nft bridge-utils
Enable and start the libvirt service:Bashsudo systemctl enable --now libvirtd
The Classic Arch Gotcha: You have to manually tell libvirt to start its default virtual network, or Vagrant will crash when it tries to attach the VMs to it:Bashsudo virsh net-autostart default
sudo virsh net-start default
Add yourself to the virtualization groups so you can run Vagrant without sudo:Bashsudo usermod -aG libvirt,kvm $USER
(Note: You must completely log out of your desktop environment and log back in right now for these group permissions to apply).Phase 2: Vagrant, Ansible & PluginsArch has Vagrant in the official repos, so you don't need to mess with HashiCorp's external PGP keys like you did on Ubuntu.Install the orchestration tools and build dependencies:Bashsudo pacman -S vagrant ansible ruby base-devel python python-virtualenv git
Install the bridge plugin so Vagrant can talk to the Linux kernel:Bashvagrant plugin install vagrant-libvirt
Phase 3: Prepping the GOAD RepositoryWe are going to use the exact same community PR branch that supports libvirt, but we are going to proactively squash that Python 3.12 ansible-core bug you hit earlier.Clone the repo and switch to the libvirt branch:Bashgit clone https://github.com/Orange-Cyberdefense/GOAD.git
cd GOAD
git fetch origin pull/475/head:libvirt-support
git checkout libvirt-support
Build the Python virtual environment:Bashpython -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
The Arch Linux Tweak: Install the GOAD requirements, but immediately force-upgrade Ansible to match Arch's bleeding-edge Python 3.12 environment, and fetch the Windows modules:Bashpip install -r requirements.yml
pip install --upgrade ansible-core
ansible-galaxy install -r ansible/requirements.yml
Phase 4: Build and ProvisionFrom here, the workflow is exactly the same as what you successfully executed in the cloud.Generate the Lab Files:Bashpython goad.py -t install -l GOAD -p libvirt
Boot the VMs: Navigate to the newly created workspace folder (e.g., cd workspace/xxxxxx-goad-libvirt/provider). If your local PC has plenty of CPU cores (8+), you can drop the --no-parallel flag and let them all boot at once!Bashvagrant up
Provision the Active Directory Forest:
Once Vagrant drops you back at the command prompt and all VMs are listening on WinRM, head back to the main GOAD directory, launch the interactive console, and fire the final script:Bashcd ~/GOAD
python goad.py
At the GOAD > prompt, type:Plaintextprovision main.yml
Because your PC has direct hardware access to the virtualization chips, the machine creation phase is going to feel incredibly fast compared to the cloud!
