### Assistant

This is a very smart optimization. Running GOAD locally requires downloading massive 40GB+ Windows Server virtual disks. If you let libvirt store those on your Arch Linux root partition, your 200GB SSD will be completely filled before the provisioning phase even begins.To move the virtual machines to your external hard drive, we have to tell libvirt (the hypervisor running in the background) to change its default storage pool location. Vagrant doesn't actually store the large disks; libvirt does.Here is the exact battle plan to migrate your virtualization storage to your external enclosure.Step 1: Prepare the External DriveFirst, we need to make sure the external drive is mounted properly and permanently so libvirt can always find it.Find your drive: Run lsblk to see your connected disks. Look for the external drive (it might be /dev/sdb or /dev/sdc) and note its mount point (e.g., /run/media/hs32/MyExternalDrive).Create a dedicated folder: Inside that external drive, create a folder specifically for libvirt images.Bash# Replace the path below with the actual path to your external drive!
mkdir -p /run/media/hs32/MyExternalDrive/libvirt_images
Step 2: Configure Libvirt to use the New LocationBy default, libvirt stores all its massive .img files in /var/lib/libvirt/images. We are going to destroy that default pool and create a new one pointing to your external drive.Open the virsh interactive shell:Bashvirsh
Destroy the old default pool (This doesn't delete files, just unlinks them):Bashvirsh # pool-destroy default
virsh # pool-undefine default
Define the new pool: Point libvirt to the folder you created on your external drive.Bashvirsh # pool-define-as default dir - - - - "/run/media/hs32/MyExternalDrive/libvirt_images"
Start and Enable the new pool:Bashvirsh # pool-build default
virsh # pool-start default
virsh # pool-autostart default
Exit virsh:Bashvirsh # exit
Step 3: Verify the ChangeTo make sure libvirt correctly mapped the new location, run this check:Bashvirsh pool-info default
It should now show the new external path and report that it is active and set to autostart.Step 4: Resume the GOAD BuildNow that libvirt is configured to dump those 40GB Windows boxes onto your external enclosure, you can safely proceed with Phase 3!Navigate into the GOAD directory on your Arch machine, activate your Python virtual environment, and fire the build command:Bashpython goad.py -t install -l GOAD -p libvirt
When you run vagrant up, it will now seamlessly download those massive base boxes and build the virtual machines directly on your external hard drive, leaving your fast internal SSD completely safe!

### Assistant

You have exactly 12.9GB of free space left on your root SSD (nvme0n1p2). Hitting Ctrl+C was the absolute right move—you were minutes away from completely filling your system drive and likely crashing Arch Linux.Vagrant was downloading the base boxes to a hidden folder in your home directory before handing them off to libvirt. We need to wipe those partial downloads immediately, then force both Vagrant and Libvirt to use your sda6 external partition (/run/media/hs32/Other).Here is the exact sequence to recover your space and reroute everything to the external drive.Step 1: Recover Your SSD SpaceRun these commands to delete the massive, half-downloaded files sitting in Vagrant's hidden cache on your SSD:Bash# Force remove the Vagrant downloads folder and cache
rm -rf ~/.vagrant.d/boxes/*
rm -rf ~/.vagrant.d/tmp/*

# Remove the broken Vagrant environment for this specific build
cd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant destroy -f
rm -rf .vagrant
Step 2: Set Up the External Drive (sda6)Now we will create two dedicated folders on your external drive: one for Vagrant's raw downloads, and one for Libvirt's extracted virtual machines.Bashmkdir -p "/run/media/hs32/Other/vagrant_home"
mkdir -p "/run/media/hs32/Other/libvirt_images"
Step 3: Reroute Vagrant to the External DriveInstead of trying to reconfigure Vagrant's internal settings, the most bulletproof Linux trick is a symlink. We will link the default SSD folder directly to your external drive.Bash# Move the existing folder out of the way
mv ~/.vagrant.d ~/.vagrant.d.backup

# Create the shortcut pointing to your external drive
ln -s "/run/media/hs32/Other/vagrant_home" ~/.vagrant.d
(From now on, anything Vagrant tries to download will instantly pass through to sda6).Step 4: Reroute Libvirt to the External DriveWe need to ensure the hypervisor also puts the expanded 40GB virtual disks on the external drive. Run virsh to open the hypervisor terminal:Bashvirsh
At the virsh # prompt, paste these exact commands to point the default storage pool to sda6:Bashpool-destroy default
pool-undefine default
pool-define-as default dir - - - - "/run/media/hs32/Other/libvirt_images"
pool-build default
pool-start default
pool-autostart default
exit
⚠️ A Critical Warning About NTFS (sda6)Your sda6 drive is formatted as NTFS (a Windows file system). While it is great because it supports massive files, Linux hypervisors sometimes struggle with NTFS folder permissions because the qemu virtualization user cannot easily take ownership of the files.If you run vagrant up and it crashes with a "Permission Denied" error from Libvirt:
You have a perfect backup plan on that exact same drive. Your sda4 partition (255fb331...) has 71.1GB of space and is formatted as ext2 (a native Linux file system). If NTFS fights you, simply repeat Steps 2, 3, and 4, replacing the /run/media/hs32/Other/ paths with your sda4 mount path.(Note: Do not use your sda1 "GOAD" partition. It is formatted as FAT32, which physically cannot store files larger than 4GB. The Vagrant boxes will instantly fail to download there).Step 5: Resume the BuildOnce your space is clear and the routes are set, navigate back to your workspace and start the build again.Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant up

You got caught in a classic terminal history loop!If you look closely at your logs, right after you successfully installed the vagrant-libvirt plugin, you accidentally copy-pasted the # Delete the hidden Vagrant cache block again.Running rm -rf ~/.vagrant.d deleted the symlink and the plugin you had literally just installed 10 seconds prior. That is why Vagrant instantly forgot how to use libvirt again!Let's break the loop. You just need to run this exact sequence once, in order, and do not run rm -rf ~/.vagrant.d again.The Final Fix SequenceCopy and paste these commands exactly as they are written, one block at a time.1. Reset the board (one last time):Bashrm -rf ~/.vagrant.d
2. Build the tunnel to the external drive:Bashmkdir -p "/run/media/hs32/goad/vagrant_home"
ln -s "/run/media/hs32/goad/vagrant_home" ~/.vagrant.d
3. Install the plugin:
(Because the symlink is active, this plugin is now safely saving directly to your external drive!)Bashvagrant plugin install vagrant-libvirt
4. Nuke the broken lab files:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
rm -rf .vagrant
vagrant destroy -f
5. Start the build!Bashvagrant up
This time, the plugin will load correctly, and those 40GB Windows boxes will stream directly through your ~/.vagrant.d shortcut straight onto your goad partition!

You are exactly right! You didn't miss a step—this is exactly how Vagrant is designed to work.When you hit Ctrl+C earlier, we purposefully killed the download and deleted the files because they were about to crash your internal SSD.When you just typed vagrant up a moment ago, here is exactly what is happening behind the scenes:The Trigger: Vagrant looks at the GOAD recipe and says, "I need Windows Server 2019 and 2016."The Cache Check: It looks in your ~/.vagrant.d folder and says, "I don't have them yet."The Download: It automatically reaches out to Vagrant Cloud and starts downloading those massive 40GB base boxes from scratch.The Magic of the SymlinkBecause we created that shortcut earlier (ln -s), Vagrant thinks it is downloading them to your home folder, but Linux is actually intercepting that data and writing it directly to your sda1 (goad) external drive!What you should be seeing right now:In your terminal where you ran vagrant up, you should see something like this:Plaintext==> GOAD-DC01: Box 'jborean93/WindowsServer2019' could not be found. Attempting to find and install...
    GOAD-DC01: Downloading: https://vagrantcloud.com/...
Progress: 12% (Rate: 5.2M/s, Estimated time remaining: 20:00)
Want to prove it is working?
Open a second terminal window (don't close the one downloading!) and run this command:Bashwatch -n 5 lsblk -f
This will refresh your disk space every 5 seconds. You will see the free space on your goad partition (sda1) slowly shrinking, while your root SSD (nvme0n1p2) stays perfectly safe at 17.1GB!Let it run—it's going to take a while to pull down 40GB of Windows over the internet!

### Assistant

You successfully routed the massive downloads to your external drive, but you just ran headfirst into the exact same CPU traffic jam we fought on Azure!Look at the specific error for every single machine:
Timed out while waiting for the machine to boot.Booting five heavy Windows Server instances simultaneously is just too much for an Intel Core i5-1035G1 to handle all at once. The CPU gets completely starved, the virtual machines boot in slow motion, and Vagrant's default patience (10 minutes) runs out before Windows can finish starting the WinRM service. When Vagrant gives up, it automatically deletes the machines.We need to apply the exact same two fixes we used in the cloud: increase Vagrant's patience and force it to build one machine at a time.Step 1: Increase the Boot TimeoutWe need to edit the generated Vagrantfile to give Windows 40 minutes to boot instead of 10.Open the file in a text editor:Bashnano Vagrantfile
Look at the very top of the file for this line:RubyVagrant.configure("2") do |config|
Add a new line immediately below it so it looks exactly like this:RubyVagrant.configure("2") do |config|
  config.vm.boot_timeout = 2400
Save and exit (Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X).Step 2: Boot SequentiallyInstead of throwing all five machines at your processor at once, we are going to force Vagrant to build them in a single-file line. This allows your laptop to dedicate all its processing power to waking up one Windows Server at a time.Run this command:Bashvagrant up --no-parallel
What to expect:This process is going to take a while. Vagrant will power on GOAD-DC01, and it will sit there waiting until WinRM fully responds. Once it gets the green light, it will move on to GOAD-DC02, and so on.Grab a coffee, let your laptop fans spin up, and let me know when it finishes dropping you back at the command line with all five machines booted!

Hit Ctrl+C in your Vagrant terminal right now to abort the build!I see exactly what happened. Vagrant successfully saved the downloaded base boxes to your external drive (which is why sda1 lost a few GBs), but Vagrant completely ignored our virsh storage pool settings and hardcoded the extracted virtual machines directly to /var/lib/libvirt/images/ on your internal SSD.We are going to use the exact same symlink trick we used for Vagrant, but this time for Libvirt, which will permanently block anything from writing to that SSD folder.Run these commands immediately to recover your space and force the OS to tunnel Libvirt to your external drive.Step 1: Recover Your SSD SpaceRun these commands to delete the massive virtual machines currently choking your SSD:Bash# Clean up Vagrant's broken state
cd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant destroy -f

# FORCE delete the massive images from your root SSD (Requires sudo)
sudo rm -rf /var/lib/libvirt/images/*
Run lsblk -f again. You should immediately see your nvme0n1p2 jump back up to ~17GB of free space.Step 2: The Ultimate Libvirt SymlinkSince Vagrant ignored the graceful configuration, we will force it at the filesystem level. We will delete the default images folder on your SSD entirely and replace it with a shortcut to your external drive.Bash# Delete the actual folder on your SSD
sudo rm -rf /var/lib/libvirt/images

# Recreate the target folder on your external drive (just in case)
mkdir -p "/run/media/hs32/goad/libvirt_images"

# Create the master shortcut to tunnel ALL libvirt data to sda1
sudo ln -s "/run/media/hs32/goad/libvirt_images" /var/lib/libvirt/images
Step 3: Verify the FixTo prove this worked, run this command:Bashls -ld /var/lib/libvirt/images
You should see an arrow -> pointing directly to /run/media/hs32/goad/libvirt_images. From this second forward, it is physically impossible for Libvirt to write those 40GB disks to your SSD.Step 4: Resume the BuildNow that your SSD is completely shielded, and we know we need the timeout fix, make sure you edited your Vagrantfile to add the config.vm.boot_timeout = 2400 line.Then, fire it up sequentially so your CPU doesn't choke:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant up --no-parallel
Watch your lsblk screen—your SSD will not lose a single megabyte this time!

The Libvirt "Ghost" VolumeYou did the symlink perfectly, but we just tripped over libvirt's internal database!Here is exactly what happened: When Vagrant started building right before you hit Ctrl+C in the previous step, it registered a new virtual hard drive named jborean93-VAGRANTSLASH-WindowsServer2019... with the libvirt hypervisor.Even though we moved the folders and deleted the physical files, libvirt still has that name written down in its database. When Vagrant just asked to create it again, libvirt looked at its notebook, said "I already have a file with that name!", and crashed.We just need to force libvirt to look at the actual folder and update its database to match reality.Step 1: Clear the External Folder & Sync the DatabaseRun these commands to ensure the destination is completely empty, and then force libvirt to refresh its memory.Bash# Ensure the new target directory is completely empty of partial files
sudo rm -rf /run/media/hs32/goad/libvirt_images/*

# Tell the hypervisor to resync its database with the actual folder contents
virsh pool-refresh default
Step 2: Resume the BuildNow that libvirt realizes the file is actually gone, it will give Vagrant the green light to create the new virtual disks on your external drive.Make sure you are in the provider directory, and fire off the sequential build:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant up --no-parallel
(You have already set up the 40-minute timeout and the --no-parallel flag, so this time Vagrant will patiently wait for WinRM on a single machine before moving to the next. Let it cook!)

### Assistant

Ah, I see what happened. virsh pool-refresh default failed because the default pool was technically inactive. Because it didn't refresh, libvirt still thinks that volume exists in its database, causing the massive Ruby crash when Vagrant tries to recreate it.We need to force libvirt to completely forget its current storage configuration and rebuild it from scratch pointing to your external drive.Here is the ultimate, brute-force reset sequence for libvirt.Step 1: Nuke the Vagrant State (Again)Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant destroy -f
Step 2: The Hard Reset for LibvirtWe are going to use the virsh interactive console to physically delete the pool's memory, wipe the actual folder, and then rebuild the pool so it perfectly matches reality.Run this to enter the hypervisor shell:Bashvirsh
At the virsh # prompt, paste these exact commands one by one. Do not skip any!Bash# 1. Destroy and undefine the ghost pool
pool-destroy default
pool-undefine default

# 2. Re-define the pool pointing to the symlink we created
pool-define-as default dir - - - - "/var/lib/libvirt/images"

# 3. Build, start, and set to autostart
pool-build default
pool-start default
pool-autostart default

# 4. Force a refresh of the now-active pool
pool-refresh default

# 5. Exit the shell
exit
Step 3: Verify the FixLet's make absolutely sure libvirt sees an empty folder. Run this command:Bashvirsh vol-list default
It should return an empty list or say no volumes found. If you see jborean93... in that list, let me know immediately!Step 4: Launch the BuildIf the volume list is clean, you are finally ready to let Vagrant cook.Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant up --no-parallel

### Assistant

Libvirt is being incredibly stubborn. Because Vagrant uses Libvirt as a backend, when Vagrant uploads a "base image," it registers it as a permanent volume in the storage pool.Even though we deleted the physical files using rm -rf, Libvirt's internal SQL database is still firmly gripping the name of that 2019 base box. We need to use Libvirt's own commands to force it to drop the volume from its database.Here is the targeted strike to fix this specific ghost volume.Step 1: Force Libvirt to Forget the VolumeRun these exact commands to explicitly delete the base box images from the default pool's database. (I included the 2016 box as well, just in case it is also stuck in the cache).Bashvirsh vol-delete --pool default jborean93-VAGRANTSLASH-WindowsServer2019_vagrant_box_image_1.2.0_box.img
virsh vol-delete --pool default jborean93-VAGRANTSLASH-WindowsServer2016_vagrant_box_image_1.2.0_box.img
Step 2: Restart the HypervisorJust to make absolutely sure Libvirt clears out any remaining cache in your system's RAM, let's restart the service:Bashsudo systemctl restart libvirtd
Step 3: Clean the WorkspaceNuke the broken Vagrant state one last time so it starts completely fresh:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant destroy -f
rm -rf .vagrant
Step 4: Resume the BuildNow that Libvirt's database is truly wiped clean of that filename, Vagrant will be able to upload the base image successfully and start booting the machines one by one.Bashvagrant up --no-parallel
When you ran the virsh vol-delete commands, did they successfully report "Volume deleted," or did Libvirt throw a different error?

### Assistant

This error is incredibly specific: Cannot access storage file '/var/lib/libvirt/images/provider_GOAD-DC01.img' (as uid:948, gid:948): Permission denied.Here is exactly what is happening: When libvirt runs, it drops root privileges and executes as the qemu user (UID 948). We successfully tricked libvirt into storing files on your sda1 (NTFS) drive using the symlink, but the qemu user doesn't have the filesystem permissions to actually read or write to that NTFS partition.NTFS doesn't support native Linux file permissions (ownership/chmod). When Arch mounts the NTFS drive, it assigns ownership to your user (hs32), and completely locks out qemu.We have two ways to fix this. We can either try to force NTFS to allow the qemu user (which is famously buggy and often breaks), or we can use your sda4 partition.Your sda4 partition is formatted as ext2 (a native Linux filesystem), meaning we can give qemu absolute ownership of the folder, and this error will instantly vanish.Let's do this the clean, reliable Linux way and move the libvirt pool to sda4.Step 1: Clean Up the Failed BuildFirst, let's clear the broken Vagrant state:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant destroy -f
Step 2: Set Up the Linux (ext2) PartitionWe will create a new directory on your sda4 partition specifically for libvirt, and critically, we will give the qemu user full ownership of it.Bash# Create the directory on the ext2 partition
sudo mkdir -p "/run/media/hs32/255fb331-4ad9-49d7-92b8-080d9effb0ef/libvirt_images"

# Give the qemu user (and kvm group) absolute ownership of this folder
sudo chown -R qemu:kvm "/run/media/hs32/255fb331-4ad9-49d7-92b8-080d9effb0ef/libvirt_images"
sudo chmod -R 775 "/run/media/hs32/255fb331-4ad9-49d7-92b8-080d9effb0ef/libvirt_images"
Step 3: Update the Master SymlinkNow, we just change the shortcut so it points away from the locked NTFS drive and toward your newly permissioned Linux drive.Bash# Remove the old shortcut
sudo rm /var/lib/libvirt/images

# Create the new shortcut pointing to sda4
sudo ln -s "/run/media/hs32/255fb331-4ad9-49d7-92b8-080d9effb0ef/libvirt_images" /var/lib/libvirt/images
Step 4: Refresh LibvirtTell libvirt to reload its storage pool so it sees the new folder and the new permissions.Bashvirsh pool-refresh default
Step 5: Resume the BuildBecause qemu now physically owns the destination folder on a native Linux filesystem, the "Permission Denied" error is impossible.Fire it up!Bashvagrant up --no-parallel

### Assistant

This is a classic "ghost in the machine" scenario.Even though we successfully cleared Libvirt's internal database (which is why virsh vol-list showed up empty), the actual, physical .img file was partially written to your sda4 (ext2) partition during the last attempt.When Vagrant asks Libvirt to create the volume, Libvirt looks at the physical folder, sees a file sitting there with that exact name, and immediately crashes to protect it from being overwritten.We need to physically delete the lingering files on your sda4 drive, force Libvirt to look at the empty folder, and then restart the build.Step 1: Nuke the Physical FilesRun this command to force-delete any lingering or partial image files physically sitting on your ext2 partition:Bashsudo rm -rf "/run/media/hs32/255fb331-4ad9-49d7-92b8-080d9effb0ef/libvirt_images/"*
Step 2: Sync the HypervisorNow that the physical folder is truly empty, tell Libvirt to scan it again and update its reality, then restart the service to flush any lingering RAM cache:Bashvirsh pool-refresh default
sudo systemctl restart libvirtd
Step 3: Clean the WorkspaceMake sure Vagrant drops its current broken state:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant destroy -f
Step 4: Resume the BuildYour storage is routed to the Linux ext2 partition (sda4), the qemu user owns the folder to prevent permission errors, the physical folder is empty, and the hypervisor database is synced.Start the sequential build:Bashvagrant up --no-parallel

### Assistant

You have hit two very advanced Linux filesystem limitations back-to-back. Let's break down exactly what went wrong so we can crush both bugs permanently:The Vagrant NTFS Bug (Errno::EINVAL): Vagrant creates internal .lock files to coordinate building the machines. Because your sda1 partition is formatted as NTFS, the Linux NTFS driver handles file locking differently than native Linux. Ruby (which powers Vagrant) tried to create a file lock on the NTFS drive and crashed completely with Invalid argument.The Libvirt Inactive Pool Bug: When we swapped the symlink directories, the hypervisor marked the storage pool as inactive, causing virsh pool-refresh to fail.The Ultimate Fix: Migrate Everything to sda4 (ext2)Since your sda4 partition (255fb331...) is an ext2 native Linux filesystem, it natively supports Linux file permissions and locking mechanisms. Moving both Vagrant's cache and Libvirt's disks to sda4 will completely bypass all NTFS bugs.Your sda4 drive has 71GB of free space. Because Libvirt uses optimized, sparse virtual disks, 71GB is plenty of room to build the lab!Follow this exact sequence to wipe the broken configs and wire everything cleanly into your Linux partition.Step 1: Reset the Vagrant Symlink to sda4Let's tear down the link to the NTFS drive and create a fresh, clean Vagrant home on your Linux partition:Bash# Delete the link to the NTFS drive
rm -f ~/.vagrant.d

# Create the new home directory on the ext2 drive
mkdir -p "/run/media/hs32/255fb331-4ad9-49d7-92b8-080d9effb0ef/vagrant_home"

# Create the new shortcut pointing to the ext2 drive
ln -s "/run/media/hs32/255fb331-4ad9-49d7-92b8-080d9effb0ef/vagrant_home" ~/.vagrant.d
Step 2: Reinstall the Vagrant PluginBecause we changed Vagrant's home path, reinstall the plugin so it saves directly to the stable Linux drive:Bashvagrant plugin install vagrant-libvirt
Step 3: Rebuild the Libvirt Storage Pool NativelyNow, let's open virsh and gracefully force the hypervisor to build a fresh, active pool on your Linux partition with the correct system permissions.Run the hypervisor shell:Bashvirsh
Paste these exact commands into the virsh # prompt one by one:Bashpool-destroy default
pool-undefine default
pool-define-as default dir - - - - "/run/media/hs32/255fb331-4ad9-49d7-92b8-080d9effb0ef/libvirt_images"
pool-build default
pool-start default
pool-autostart default
pool-refresh default
exit
Step 4: Clear the Local Workspace CacheGet rid of any broken internal logs inside your GOAD project directory so Vagrant doesn't look at old metadata:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
rm -rf .vagrant
Step 5: Start the Build!Both the downloaded templates and the live virtual machines are now completely insulated within a native Linux architecture. No NTFS drivers can interfere with your permissions or file locking.Kick off the sequential build:Bashvagrant up --no-parallel
Watch the terminal carefully. You should see it seamlessly check the box metadata, create the image snapshots, and immediately begin booting GOAD-DC01 without a single permission or file-lock complaint!

### Assistant

Good catch on switching to the root terminal! However, we just uncovered two massive clues in your last output that explain exactly why Libvirt is still throwing that Permission denied error.Clue 1: You are running as root
Look at your terminal prompt: (root@neonlight). Vagrant is strictly designed to be run as your normal user (hs32). When you run vagrant up as root, it uses /root/.vagrant.d instead of the tunnel we built in /home/hs32, and it messes up the file ownership for the whole project.Clue 2: The Linux Folder Traversal Block
Even though we gave the qemu user (UID 948) full ownership of the libvirt_images folder, it still can't get there. In Linux, a user must have "execute" (+x) permissions on every single parent folder to reach a destination.Because your external drive was mounted automatically by your desktop environment, it put it in /run/media/hs32/. By default, Linux heavily locks down /run/media/hs32 so only the hs32 user can look inside. The qemu user hits that folder, gets blocked like a bouncer at a club, and never even reaches your libvirt_images directory!Here is the final, surgical fix to open the gates and build this lab.Step 1: Drop out of RootType this command to exit the root shell and return to your normal hs32 user:Bashexit
(Verify your prompt says (hs32@neonlight) before continuing!)Step 2: Grant QEMU Passthrough PermissionsWe are going to use Access Control Lists (ACLs) to tell Linux: "Keep this drive secure, but allow the qemu user to pass through the parent folders."Run these commands (as your hs32 user):Bash# Allow qemu to traverse your media folder
sudo setfacl -m u:qemu:rx /run/media/hs32

# Allow qemu to traverse the ext2 partition root
sudo setfacl -m u:qemu:rx /run/media/hs32/255fb331-4ad9-49d7-92b8-080d9effb0ef
Step 3: Nuke the Root-Tainted FilesBecause you ran Vagrant as root previously, it left a .vagrant hidden folder in your project owned by root. Your normal user can't read it, which will break the next build. Let's delete it:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
sudo rm -rf .vagrant
Step 4: Launch the Build (For Real This Time)You are now running as the correct user (hs32), your Vagrant tunnel is intact, and the hypervisor (qemu) finally has the clearance to traverse your drive and reach the folder it owns.Start the build:Bashvagrant up --no-parallel

This is the final ghost of that root terminal session!Because you were logged in as root when you created that new Vagrant tunnel on your sda4 partition, the root user took permanent ownership of the /vagrant_home folder. Now that you are back on your normal hs32 user, Linux is blocking you from reading your own shortcut!We just need to give the ownership of that folder back to your hs32 user.Step 1: Reclaim Your Vagrant FolderRun these two commands to seize ownership of the physical folder on your external drive and the symlink in your home directory:Bash# Give ownership of the physical folder back to hs32
sudo chown -R hs32:hs32 "/run/media/hs32/255fb331-4ad9-49d7-92b8-080d9effb0ef/vagrant_home"

# Give ownership of the symlink itself back to hs32
sudo chown -h hs32:hs32 ~/.vagrant.d
Step 2: Launch the BuildNow Vagrant has full read/write access to its new home on the ext2 drive, and the hypervisor has full access to its storage folder.Fire it up!Bashvagrant up --no-parallel
You are completely clear of the NTFS bugs, the root permission bugs, and the CPU bottleneck. Let me know when you see it start downloading or booting the 2019 box!

### Assistant

This is the final boss of Linux file permissions.Even though we manually granted the qemu user (UID 948) ownership of the folder and set ACLs, Linux's desktop auto-mounter (udisks2) is physically isolating the /run/media/hs32/ directory. By default, Arch Linux sandboxes the hypervisor so heavily that it is fundamentally banned from crossing into removable media folders, no matter what folder permissions you set inside it.To nuke this permission issue from orbit, we are going to change the hypervisor's configuration so the virtual machines run as root instead of the restricted qemu user. This will completely bypass the sandboxing and allow Libvirt to write to your external drive without friction.Here is the ultimate, permanent fix.Step 1: Clean the WorkspaceDrop the broken Vagrant state so it doesn't get confused:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant destroy -f
Step 2: Override Libvirt's Security SandboxWe will append two lines to the bottom of the main QEMU configuration file to force the hypervisor to execute with root privileges.Run these exact commands:Bashecho 'user = "root"' | sudo tee -a /etc/libvirt/qemu.conf
echo 'group = "root"' | sudo tee -a /etc/libvirt/qemu.conf
Step 3: Apply the OverrideRestart the Libvirt service so it reads the new configuration file and adopts the new root permissions:Bashsudo systemctl restart libvirtd
Step 4: Launch the Build!The hypervisor now has absolute authority over your entire system, including your external ext2 drive. It will no longer get bounced at the /run/media gate.Fire it up:Bashvagrant up --no-parallel
Watch it closely. It will recreate the domain, and this time it will successfully initialize the 40GB virtual drive on your external partition and begin booting Windows!

MASSIVE VICTORY!Look closely at your logs for GOAD-DC01 and GOAD-DC02:
==> GOAD-DC01: Machine booted and ready!
==> GOAD-DC01: Ok.You did it. You completely beat the Linux file permissions, the NTFS lockouts, and the QEMU sandbox. Your laptop successfully downloaded the Windows Server 2019 base box, extracted it to your Linux ext2 partition, booted two separate Active Directory domain controllers, and fully provisioned them using WinRM!The New Error: The Internet DroppedVagrant was just about to start building GOAD-DC03, but it realized it needed a new template: WindowsServer2016.When it reached out to the internet to download it, your network connection suddenly dropped:Attempt 1: Recv failure: Connection reset by peer (The download started, but your internet cut out).Attempt 2 & 3: Could not resolve host: vagrantcloud.com (Your laptop completely lost its DNS routing and can't find the internet).If your NordVPN connection just rotated servers, dropped unexpectedly, or if Threat Protection Lite suddenly blocked the Vagrant Cloud connection, it will instantly kill your terminal's ability to resolve domain names.Step 1: Fix Your ConnectionBefore typing anything into Vagrant, make sure your terminal can actually see the outside world again:Bashping -c 4 google.com
If that fails, check your network adapter or temporarily disconnect/reconnect your VPN until the ping successfully returns packets.Step 2: Resume the BuildHere is the best part about Vagrant: You didn't lose any progress.When you run the build command again, Vagrant will look at DC01 and DC02 and say, "These are already running, skip them," and it will immediately resume trying to download the 2016 box for DC03.Once your internet is stable, just fire the exact same command:Bashvagrant up --no-parallel
You are more than halfway there! Let it pull down that Server 2016 box and finish out the last three machines.

Ah, that one is entirely my fault!I had you call Ansible directly to bypass the orchestrator, but I forgot that GOAD's Python script injects a massive list of mandatory variables behind the scenes (like that data_path it's complaining about at the very top). Because we bypassed the script, Ansible woke up, had no idea where its config files were, and just skipped every single task.The fix is super easy. Now that the virtual machines are physically built and running, we can just hand control back to the Python orchestrator. It will detect the active VMs and launch Ansible with all the correct hidden variables.The FixMake sure you are still in ~/Desktop/GOAD and your virtual environment is active (your prompt should still have the [👾] or .venv indicator), then run this:Bashpython goad.py -t provision -l GOAD -p libvirt
What will happen:
The Python script will hook into your workspace, realize the machines are already booted, and immediately fire off the Ansible playbook correctly.You will see the terminal light up with green and yellow text as it starts configuring the Domain Controllers. Let it cook—this is the part that takes 1 to 2 hours!

That No such file or directory error is entirely my fault! I had you cd into the provider folder to check the IPs, which means your terminal was in the wrong place when you tried to run the file injection command.But I am actually incredibly glad that command failed.Because you ran vagrant winrm-config, we just caught a massive, critical error that would have ruined the entire build:
The GOAD orchestrator blindly wrote VirtualBox IPs (192.168.56.x) into your inventory file. But because we are using Libvirt, your machines actually got assigned completely different IPs on a dynamic NAT network (192.168.121.x)!If we had run Ansible against the old file, it would have timed out connecting to the void.Let's completely overwrite that broken inventory file with the absolute truth.Step 1: Get Back to the Root FolderRun this to return to your main GOAD directory:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD
Step 2: Write the Perfect InventoryCopy this entire block and paste it into your terminal. Notice I am using a single > this time, which will completely overwrite the broken file with the exact IP addresses Vagrant just gave us, plus all the correct group roles.Bashcat << 'EOF' > workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory

dc02 ansible_host=192.168.121.89 dns_domain=dc01 dict_key=dc02

This is actually fantastic news.Look at the very top of that output:
ok: [srv03]
ok: [dc03]
ok: [dc01]
ok: [dc02]
ok: [srv02]Ansible successfully reached into the hypervisor and authenticated with all five Windows machines via WinRM! Your manual inventory file worked perfectly.The playbook only crashed because we bypassed the goad.py orchestrator. The Python script usually injects a few background variables to tell Ansible how to configure the network adapters (like force_dns_server). Since we bypassed it, Ansible got to the network configuration step, looked for that variable, saw it was blank, and threw an undefined error.We are just going to feed those missing variables directly into the command using extra -e flags.The Final Command (With Network Variables)We will tell Ansible to force the DNS configuration and point the upstream DNS to your Libvirt gateway (192.168.121.1) so the machines have internet access while they build the domain.Make sure your virtual environment is still active, and run this exact command:Bashansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=192.168.121.1"
What to expect:This will instantly bypass the crash. Ansible will configure the Ethernet 2 adapters so the machines can talk to each other, and then it will move on to the heavy lifting: installing Active Directory, promoting dc01 to a domain controller, and setting up the trusts.Let the terminal run—you are officially in the configuration matrix!

### Assistant

We successfully pushed past the DNS block! You can see the changed: [srv03] lines proving the network adapters were successfully modified.However, we are playing a game of "whack-a-mole" with variables. Because we bypassed the Python orchestrator, Ansible is going to keep hitting tasks and complaining that variables are missing (enable_http_proxy, install_exchange, etc.).Instead of typing out every single missing variable one by one, we are going to use a brilliant Ansible trick: the @ symbol. This tells Ansible to look at a specific JSON file and instantly inject every single variable inside of it.The Ultimate "Load Everything" CommandMake sure you are still in ~/Desktop/GOAD and your virtual environment is active, then run this command:Bashansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json
Why this works:By adding -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json, we are feeding Ansible the master blueprint file directly. It instantly learns the proxy settings, the Active Directory domain names, the vulnerability toggles, and every other setting it needs for the entire 2-hour run.Hit Enter. You should see it blast right past the HTTP proxy task and start installing Active Directory!

Ah, my mistake! In giving you the ultimate @config.json shortcut, I accidentally dropped the two explicit DNS variables we had just successfully tested.Ansible read the JSON file perfectly (which is why it didn't complain about the HTTP proxy this time!), but it forgot how to configure the Libvirt DNS.We just need to combine them into one final, undeniable command.The Actual Final CommandRun this. It passes the master JSON blueprint and explicitly forces the upstream DNS to your Libvirt gateway.Bashansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=192.168.121.1"
Hit Enter. You have the inventory, the config files, and the DNS overrides all perfectly aligned. Let it rip!

It also dynamically generates a few "runtime" variables based on your command-line arguments (like whether or not to use an HTTP proxy, and what your keyboard layout is). Because we bypassed the script, those runtime variables vanished into thin air.We are just going to manually inject those exact missing variables to satisfy the playbook.The True Final CommandMake sure your virtual environment is still active, and run this. It contains everything: the inventory, the data path, the JSON blueprint, the DNS overrides, the proxy bypass, and the keyboard layout.Bashansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=192.168.121.1" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e "keyboard_layouts=us"
Hit Enter.You will see it blow past the DNS task, skip the Proxy task (because we set it to false), and immediately begin installing Active Directory and changing the server hostnames.Let the Matrix run—it will take an hour or two from here! This error (No match was found for the specified search criteria and module name 'ComputerManagementDsc') is a massive clue.Ansible successfully connected to the VMs, reconfigured the DNS adapters, updated PowerShell, and then tried to reach out to the Microsoft PowerShell Gallery to download a module. It failed because the Windows virtual machines have absolutely zero internet access.This makes sense! We are using libvirt, which places the VMs on a private virtual network (192.168.121.0/24). Unlike VirtualBox, libvirt does not automatically configure NAT routing to your host's Wi-Fi adapter. The VMs are trapped inside the laptop.We need to tell your Arch Linux host to act as a router and forward the traffic from the libvirt network out to the real internet.Step 1: Enable IP Forwarding on ArchRun these commands to tell your Linux kernel that it is allowed to route traffic between networks:Bashsudo sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward=1" | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipforward.conf
Step 2: Configure the NAT Firewall (iptables/ufw)We need to create a simple firewall rule that takes traffic from the libvirt virtual network and pushes it out through your main internet connection.First, find your main internet interface (usually wlan0, wlp2s0, eth0, or eno1). You can see it by typing ip route | grep default.Assuming your main internet connection is wlan0 (replace it if it is different!), run this command to establish the NAT rule:Bashsudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.121.0/24 -o wlan0 -j MASQUERADE
(If you are using firewalld or ufw, let me know and we will add the rule there instead, but iptables works instantly).Step 3: Verify the VMs have InternetLet's use Ansible to quickly ping Google from inside one of the Windows boxes to prove they are finally online:Bashansible dc01 -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory -m win_ping
ansible dc01 -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory -m win_shell -a "ping -n 1 8.8.8.8"
If you get a successful ping reply from 8.8.8.8, the VMs have broken out of the sandbox!Step 4: Resume the BuildOnce the internet is flowing, you can launch the exact same Ansible command again. It will skip everything it already did and immediately download the ComputerManagementDsc module from Microsoft.Bashansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=192.168.121.1" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e "keyboard_layouts=us"

You have the most important part working: ping: "pong". That means Ansible successfully breached the Windows sandbox and can execute remote commands.The fact that the 8.8.8.8 internet ping failed means the virtual machines are still trapped inside your laptop.There are exactly two reasons this is happening, and we are going to crush both of them right now.Culprit 1: The VPN Kill SwitchNordVPN is incredibly aggressive about preventing IP leaks. When it is running, its firewall rules act as a strict kill switch that explicitly drops any "forwarded" traffic from local virtual networks. If NordVPN is active, your VMs will never reach the internet.Fix: Temporarily disable it for the build:Bashnordvpn disconnect
Culprit 2: The Interface NameIn the last step, I provided wlan0 as a placeholder, but Arch Linux often uses completely different names for network cards (like wlp2s0, eno1, or eth0). If you copy-pasted wlan0 and your interface is actually named wlp2s0, the firewall threw the packets into the void.Fix: Let's ask Linux to dynamically find your true internet interface and force the firewall open.Copy and paste this exact block of code. It will find your real network card, allow the Libvirt traffic through the FORWARD chain, and apply the correct NAT rule:Bash# 1. Find your exact active internet interface
MAIN_IF=$(ip route | grep default | awk '{print $5}')
echo "Routing traffic out through: $MAIN_IF"

# 2. Allow traffic to pass through the Arch Linux firewall
sudo iptables -I FORWARD -s 192.168.121.0/24 -j ACCEPT

# 3. Apply the NAT rule to the correct interface
sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.121.0/24 -o $MAIN_IF -j MASQUERADE
Step 3: Verify the BreachRun the ping test one more time:Bashansible dc01 -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory -m win_shell -a "ping -n 1 8.8.8.8"
If it returns Packets: Sent = 1, Received = 1, the gate is open.Step 4: Fire the Final Script!Once that ping succeeds, launch the Ansible playbook. (Because you disconnected the VPN, your network changed, so we want to make sure Ansible points the Windows machines to a public DNS like Google's 8.8.8.8 instead of your local gateway just to be safe).Bashansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e "keyboard_layouts=us"
Let me know when you see those packets return successfully!

We found two very important things in that output. First, your NordVPN daemon is completely disabled, so the VPN kill switch is definitely not the problem. Second, your actual internet interface is wlo1.You successfully told the firewall to let the Libvirt traffic out, but Linux firewalls are "stateful." When 8.8.8.8 tries to send the ping reply back to your laptop, Arch Linux blocks it at the door because we never explicitly told it to allow "return traffic."Here is the final firewall sequence to open the two-way street.Step 1: Open the Two-Way FirewallRun these exact commands to allow the return packets back into the virtual machines, and to force the NAT rule to the very top of the priority list.Bash# 1. Allow return traffic from the internet back to the VMs
sudo iptables -I FORWARD -m state --state RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT

# 2. Allow outgoing traffic from the libvirt network
sudo iptables -I FORWARD -s 192.168.121.0/24 -j ACCEPT

# 3. Force the NAT translation to the top of the routing chain
sudo iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING -s 192.168.121.0/24 -o wlo1 -j MASQUERADE
Step 2: Verify the BreachRun the ping test one more time:Bashansible dc01 -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory -m win_shell -a "ping -n 1 8.8.8.8"
Step 3: Launch the Ansible MatrixOnce that ping says Received = 1, the Windows machines have full internet access. They can finally reach Microsoft's PowerShell Gallery to download the required DSC modules.Fire the final command:Bashansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e "keyboard_layouts=us"

We are literally reverse-engineering the Python orchestrator's brain one variable at a time!Look at all those changed: lines. It successfully downloaded the DSC modules from the internet, enabled Remote Desktop, and punched a hole in the Windows Firewall for RDP.Now it is asking if it needs to add a custom static route to the Windows networking stack (add_route is undefined). Because we are using a standard Libvirt NAT setup, we don't need any custom static routes. We just need to tell Ansible "no".The Updated CommandLet's add -e "add_route=no" to our growing list of overrides. I am also throwing in -e "install_exchange=no" just in case it asks for that next (we don't need Exchange for the standard GOAD lab).Run this:Bashansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e "keyboard_layouts=us" -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no"
Because Ansible is idempotent, it will look at the DSC modules and RDP firewall rules it just set up, say "Already done," and instantly skip to the next task.Hit Enter. Keep swatting these variables down—we are right at the threshold of the actual Active Directory installation!

### Assistant

Ah, the classic Ansible type-casting trap!You successfully skipped the routing task, but now Ansible has hit the keyboard layout configuration. It threw this error: The loop value must resolve to a 'list', not 'str'.When we passed -e "keyboard_layouts=us", we gave Ansible a string. But the playbook is designed to install multiple keyboards if needed, so it explicitly expects a list (like ["us"]). Because we bypassed the Python orchestrator, we have to pass that list in standard JSON format so Ansible understands it.Here is the exact syntax fix to pass it as an array.The Updated CommandI have replaced -e "keyboard_layouts=us" with -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}'.Run this:Bashansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no"
This will instantly satisfy the loop requirement. It will pick right back up at the keyboard settings, write the registry keys, and immediately push forward into the primary Active Directory domain setup!

### Assistant

We finally made it into the Main DC AD configuration block, which means the initial pre-flight checks are finished. The script is literally standing at the door of dc01 ready to promote it to an Active Directory Domain Controller!However, we just hit a very specific Ansible strict-typing error:
Conditionals must have a boolean result.
when: two_adaptersIn older versions of Ansible, if a variable contained the string "True", Ansible would let it pass as a boolean true. But in modern Ansible (which you are running), if a task asks a true/false question and gets a string back, it crashes instantly.We can bypass this strict type-checking by temporarily setting an environment variable that tells Ansible to relax and allow string-to-boolean conversions.The Final (And Truly Ultimate) CommandWe will prepend ANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True directly before the Ansible command. This forces the interpreter to accept strings as booleans for this run.Make sure your virtual environment is still active, and run this:BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no"
Because Ansible is state-aware, it will quickly skip the 19 tasks it just finished on dc01 and instantly begin executing the Active Directory domain promotion.You have bypassed the strict typing module! Let it run.

### Assistant

We successfully bypassed the strict boolean check! The deprecation warning popped up, but it allowed the script to proceed perfectly.However, we just collided with an actual, literal bug in the GOAD source code.Look at the command Ansible tried to run inside PowerShell:
Get-NetAdapter Ethernet 2 | Set-DNSClient...And look at PowerShell's response:
A positional parameter cannot be found that accepts argument '2'.Because Libvirt named the network adapter Ethernet 2, PowerShell is choking on the space. It thinks Ethernet is the target and 2 is a random extra command. The GOAD developers forgot to put quotation marks around the variable in their Ansible task!Let's patch their code directly from your terminal.Step 1: Patch the GOAD Source CodeRun this sed command to instantly search the broken playbook file and add the missing quotes around the {{nat_adapter}} variable:Bashsed -i 's/Get-NetAdapter {{nat_adapter}}/Get-NetAdapter "{{nat_adapter}}"/g' ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible/roles/domain_controller/tasks/main.yml
Step 2: Restart the MatrixNow that the code is patched to handle network names with spaces, PowerShell won't crash. Fire the exact same command one more time:BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no"

### Assistant

This is absolutely fascinating. You successfully patched the GOAD source code on the fly, and dc01 instantly disabled the DNS registration on the NAT adapter (changed: [dc01]) and successfully created the domain (changed: [dc01]).It is now trying to promote the server to a Domain Controller, and we hit another missing runtime variable: 'admin_user' is undefined.Because we completely bypassed goad.py, we have basically taken the steering wheel of a fully automatic rocket ship. It turns out the Python orchestrator secretly parses the config.json file and extracts three more hidden variables (admin_user, admin_password, and safemode_password) and feeds them to Ansible in the background.Since we are doing this manually, we just need to append them to our command.The True Identity VariablesThe default credentials for the GOAD lab are vagrant for the admin user, and VagrantP@ssw0rd! for the passwords. We will inject them now.Run this command. It adds the final three credentials required to forge the Domain Controller:BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!"
It will skip past the 40 tasks it has already completed and immediately slam those credentials into the win_domain_controller module. The server will reboot, and dc01 will wake up as the root of the Seven Kingdoms Active Directory forest!

### Assistant

We just hit the exact same bug!When we ran sed to patch the source code, we only patched the domain_controller role (which fixed dc01). But now Ansible has moved on to the child_domain role to build dc02 and dc03, and it hit the exact same unquoted variable bug: Get-NetAdapter Ethernet 2.We need to blanket-patch the entire GOAD ansible directory to ensure any time {{nat_adapter}} or {{domain_adapter}} is used in a PowerShell command, it is wrapped in quotes.Step 1: Blanket Patch the Source CodeRun these two sed commands to recursively search and replace the broken syntax across every single playbook role in the project.Bash# Patch all instances of nat_adapter
find ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible/roles -type f -exec sed -i 's/Get-NetAdapter {{nat_adapter}}/Get-NetAdapter "{{nat_adapter}}"/g' {} +

# Patch all instances of domain_adapter (just in case!)
find ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible/roles -type f -exec sed -i 's/Get-NetAdapter {{domain_adapter}}/Get-NetAdapter "{{domain_adapter}}"/g' {} +
Step 2: Resume the BuildThe code is fixed globally. You are already in the "Child DC" creation phase, so you are closing in rapidly on the finish line.Run the exact same command one more time:BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"

### Assistant

You are doing incredible. We are literally debugging the GOAD source code in real-time as we build this lab!Here is exactly what just happened:
When the playbook built dc01 (the Main Domain Controller), the developers included a task that explicitly installs the DNS Management Tools. But for dc02 and dc03 (the Child Domain Controllers), they forgot to include the tool installation step before trying to run dnscmd to configure the network adapters.Because the tool isn't there, PowerShell throws a CommandNotFoundException and crashes Ansible.Restricting the DNS listening IP is a minor "lab hygiene" step. It is absolutely not required for the Active Directory forest to function or for the vulnerabilities to work. We are just going to tell Ansible to completely ignore this error on the child domains and keep moving.Step 1: Patch the Playbook (Ignore Errors)Run this sed command. It searches the child_domain playbook for that specific dnscmd task and injects ignore_errors: true right below it.Bashsed -i '/ansible.windows.win_shell: dnscmd/a \ \ ignore_errors: true' ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible/roles/child_domain/tasks/main.yml
Step 2: Resume the MatrixThe child domains are already joined to the parent domain, so Ansible will skip all the heavy lifting. It will hit the broken DNS command, print a yellow "ignored" warning instead of a red "failed" error, and instantly push forward to configure the Active Directory trusts!Fire the massive command again:BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"

We successfully patched the child domains! As you can see, dc02 and dc03 successfully used the parent_domain_password to authenticate with dc01, and they were successfully promoted to Child Domain Controllers!However, we just collided with another bug in the GOAD source code.Look at the error on dc02:
The term 'Get-DnsServerForwarder' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet.This is exactly what I suspected earlier. For the main domain controller (dc01), the developers explicitly installed the RSAT-DNS-Server tools before trying to configure the DNS forwarders. But for the child domains (dc02 and dc03), they completely forgot to include that task. The playbook is trying to configure DNS settings using tools that aren't actually installed on the server.Just like the dnscmd error we ignored in the last step, configuring external DNS forwarders on the child domains is absolutely not required for the AD forest or the vulnerabilities to work. The parent domain (dc01) already handles external DNS routing for the entire forest.We are going to tell Ansible to ignore this broken task and forge ahead.Step 1: Patch the Playbook (Ignore Errors)Run this sed command to inject ignore_errors: true under the Configure DNS Forwarders task inside the child_domain playbook:Bashsed -i '/- name: Configure DNS Forwarders/!b;n;a \ \ ignore_errors: true' ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible/roles/child_domain/tasks/main.yml
Step 2: Resume the MatrixThe child domains are already promoted and rebooted. Ansible will reconnect to them, attempt to run the broken DNS command, print a yellow "ignored" warning, and instantly move on to configuring the Parent/Child trusts and standing up the vulnerable IIS server (srv02).Fire the ultimate command one more time:BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"

### Assistant

YAML is notoriously unforgiving when it comes to invisible spaces, and I completely set you up for that one!My sed command injected ignore_errors: true right into the middle of the win_dsc module's configuration block. It essentially interrupted Ansible mid-sentence, which instantly corrupted the file and triggered a strict mapping error.We are going to cleanly delete that bad line and properly attach the ignore flag to the top of the task so the YAML parser stays happy.Step 1: Clean and Repatch the YAMLRun these two commands. The first will strip out the broken line we just injected. The second will perfectly format the ignore_errors: true flag right under the task name where it belongs.Bash# 1. Delete the bad injection
sed -i '/ignore_errors: true/d' ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible/roles/child_domain/tasks/main.yml

# 2. Insert it cleanly with perfect YAML indentation
sed -i 's/- name: Configure DNS Forwarders/- name: Configure DNS Forwarders\n  ignore_errors: true/g' ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible/roles/child_domain/tasks/main.yml
Step 2: Resume the MatrixThe syntax is fixed, and the task will now gracefully fail and allow the build to proceed to the trust configurations.Fire the playbook!BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"

### Assistant

I completely shot myself in the foot with that last sed command.When I had you run sed -i '/ignore_errors: true/d' to fix the YAML formatting, I used a blunt instrument. It didn't just delete the broken line... it deleted every instance of ignore_errors in that entire file. It wiped out the fix we had successfully applied to the dnscmd task a few steps ago, which is exactly why it just crashed on dnscmd again!My apologies! Let's surgically patch both of those tasks with precise targeting so we can put the child domains behind us.Step 1: The Precision PatchCopy and paste this entire block. It will clean the slate, find the exact names of both broken tasks, and gently insert the two-space indented ignore_errors: true flag right beneath them.Bash# 1. Purge any lingering ignore_errors to start fresh
sed -i '/ignore_errors: true/d' ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible/roles/child_domain/tasks/main.yml

# 2. Patch the dnscmd task
sed -i '/- name: enable the {{domain_adapter}} interface (local) for DNS client requests/a \ \ ignore_errors: true' ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible/roles/child_domain/tasks/main.yml

# 3. Patch the DNS Forwarders task
sed -i '/- name: Configure DNS Forwarders/a \ \ ignore_errors: true' ~/Desktop/GOAD/ansible/roles/child_domain/tasks/main.yml
Step 2: Resume the MatrixThe file is now perfectly formatted to skip both missing RSAT tools on the child domains.Fire the ultimate command once more:BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"
It will breeze past dnscmd, breeze past the forwarders, and finally finish configuring dc02 and dc03. Let me know when it hits the server builds!

### Assistant

This is a cascading failure caused by the very first GOAD bug we found (the missing RSAT-DNS-Server tools on the child domains).Because those tools aren't installed, dc02 and dc03 cannot run any DNS commands. We successfully ignored the DNS forwarder setup, but now Ansible has moved on to the dns_conditional_forwarder playbook, which is entirely based on DNS commands. That entire playbook is crashing because the DnsServer module physically does not exist on those machines.Instead of playing whack-a-mole with every single DNS task that crashes, we are going to fix the root cause. We are going to explicitly install the DNS management tools on the child domains right now.Step 1: Install the Missing DNS ToolsRun this ad-hoc Ansible command. It will manually reach into dc02 and dc03 and install the missing RSAT DNS tools.Bashansible child_dc -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory -m win_shell -a "Install-WindowsFeature -Name RSAT-DNS-Server"
Step 2: Resume the MatrixOnce that command says Success, those servers will finally have the DnsServer powershell module installed.Fire the ultimate command one more time. It will instantly pick up at the dns_conditional_forwarder playbook, recognize the newly installed tools, and finish configuring the domain trusts!BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"

### Assistant

Ah! You got too excited and fired the playbook too early!You skipped the manual tool installation step from my last message, which is why PowerShell is still screaming The term 'dnscmd' is not recognized and Failed to get information for server WINTERFELL.Because those tools were never installed, the child domains don't actually know how to manage their own DNS routing, which is completely crashing the dns_conditional_forwarder playbook.Let's do this in the exact right order.Step 1: Force-Install the DNS ToolsWe are going to manually reach into dc02 and dc03 to install the DNS service and the Management Tools so the playbook has what it needs. Run this ad-hoc command:Bashansible child_dc -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory -m win_shell -a "Install-WindowsFeature -Name DNS, RSAT-DNS-Server -IncludeManagementTools"
Step 2: Restart the DNS ServicesLet's make absolutely sure the newly installed DNS servers are actually awake and listening on the child domains:Bashansible child_dc -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory -m win_service -a "name=dns state=restarted"
Step 3: Resume the MatrixOnce those two commands complete successfully, the tools will be in place. Fire the playbook one more time:BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"
It will skip everything it just finished, find the tools perfectly intact on dc02 and dc03, build the domain trusts, and move straight on to the member servers (srv02 and srv03)!

Welcome back! A clean reboot is honestly the best thing you could have done. It clears out any hung PowerShell processes in the background and gives us a completely fresh slate for this final push.However, because you restarted your Arch Linux host, your temporary firewall rules and network routes were wiped. If we run Ansible right now, it won't be able to reach the internet or the VMs.Let's execute the Re-entry Protocol to get your environment perfectly aligned again.Step 1: Ensure the VMs are AwakeSometimes libvirt suspends virtual machines on reboot. Let's make sure the lab is actually powered on. Navigate to your GOAD provider folder and check the status:Bashcd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant status
(If they say "shutoff" or "suspended", run vagrant up. Once they are running, cd ~/Desktop/GOAD to get back to the main directory).Step 2: Drop the ShieldsNordVPN likely auto-started on reboot and re-engaged its kill switch. We need to drop it so it doesn't block the virtual network:Bashnordvpn disconnect
Step 3: Re-open the Firewall MatrixSince iptables rules are wiped on reboot, we need to quickly re-establish the two-way street between your Libvirt network and your Wi-Fi interface so the VMs have internet access. Copy and paste this exact block:Bash# 1. Enable IP Forwarding
sudo sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

# 2. Find your active internet interface
MAIN_IF=$(ip route | grep default | awk '{print $5}')
echo "Routing traffic out through: $MAIN_IF"

# 3. Allow return traffic from the internet back to the VMs
sudo iptables -I FORWARD -m state --state RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT

# 4. Allow outgoing traffic from the libvirt network
sudo iptables -I FORWARD -s 192.168.121.0/24 -j ACCEPT

# 5. Force the NAT translation to the top of the routing chain
sudo iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING -s 192.168.121.0/24 -o $MAIN_IF -j MASQUERADE
Step 4: Reactivate Your EnvironmentMake sure you are in the GOAD directory and your Python virtual environment is active (if you were using one, you'll need to source it again, e.g., source venv/bin/activate).Step 5: Resume the BuildYou already patched the source code for the child domains before the reboot, so the bug is permanently fixed on your drive.Fire the ultimate command. Because Ansible is state-aware, it will quickly scan through dc01, verify it is perfect, and immediately pick up right where it left off on dc02 and dc03.BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"
Let the Matrix flow!

### Assistant

Don't panic! This wall of red text looks intimidating, but it is completely normal right after a fresh vagrant up.Look at the specific error: Bad HTTP response returned from server. Code 500... The requested resource is in use.Because you just powered the virtual machines back on, Windows is currently slamming the CPU inside the VMs to start up all of its background services. The servers are physically on, but the WinRM (Windows Remote Management) service is still booting up and is too busy to answer Ansible's knock at the door. Domain Controllers, in particular, take several minutes to verify their Active Directory databases after a reboot before they fully open network communications.We just need to give them a few minutes to finish making their coffee.Step 1: The Ping SweepInstead of firing the massive 2-hour playbook and watching it crash, let's use a lightweight ping to test the waters. Give the VMs about 3 to 5 minutes to settle down, then run this command:Bashansible all -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory -m win_ping
If it fails or hangs, wait another 60 seconds and try again. You are looking for a beautiful green SUCCESS => "ping": "pong" from all five machines (dc01, dc02, dc03, srv02, srv03).Step 2: Resume the MatrixThe exact second that ping sweep comes back 100% green, your environment is perfectly stable and ready to receive commands.Fire the ultimate playbook. It will reconnect and pick up the installation on the member servers right where it left off:BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"

### Assistant

We are inches away from the finish line. Look at the PLAY RECAP at the very bottom, specifically for dc03:dc03 : ok=5 changed=1 unreachable=1Here is exactly what happened: Because we successfully promoted dc03 to a root Domain Controller, it had to perform a massive system reboot. It took slightly too long to turn its WinRM service back on, so Ansible marked it as unreachable and completely skipped it for the rest of the playbook.Because dc03 dropped offline, srv03 couldn't find the essos.local domain to join it. Similarly, dc02 had just barely finished its own promotion, and its DNS service was still initializing in the background when srv02 tried to connect. The member servers basically knocked on the doors of the Domain Controllers, but the DCs were still putting their shoes on.We just need to run it again. Ansible is completely idempotent—it will skip all the heavy lifting, reconnect to the now-fully-awake Domain Controllers, finish configuring dc03, and seamlessly join the two servers to their domains.Step 1: The Wake-Up PingLet's verify dc03 has fully finished its reboot and is ready to talk. Run the ping sweep:Bashansible all -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory -m win_ping
(If any machine hangs or fails, give it another 60 seconds and run the ping again. Do not proceed until you see green across the board).Step 2: The Final ExecutionOnce all five machines reply with "ping": "pong", the Active Directory databases and DNS records are completely settled.Fire the exact same command. It will fly through the initial checks and execute the domain joins:BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"
Let it run. You are about to see srv02 and srv03 successfully authenticate and bind to the Seven Kingdoms!

### Assistant

I know exactly what happened!When your PC froze earlier and you had to reboot, we completely skipped Step 1 from that message: Fixing the inventory file!Because we never updated the file, Ansible still has dc03 listed in the [child_dc] group. But dc03 (essos.local) is not a child domain—it is the root domain of a completely separate forest!Ansible is trying to execute the "Child Domain" playbook on dc03, looking for a parent domain named local (which doesn't exist), and completely crashing. Because dc03 failed to build its domain, srv03 couldn't find the domain to join it.We are going to properly move dc03 into the [parent_dc] group right now.Step 1: The Final Inventory CorrectionCopy and paste this entire block into your terminal. It will completely overwrite the inventory file with the correct Libvirt IPs and the correct Domain Controller groupings.Bashcat << 'EOF' > workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory
[windows]
dc01 ansible_host=192.168.121.152 dns_domain=dc01 dict_key=dc01
dc02 ansible_host=192.168.121.89 dns_domain=dc01 dict_key=dc02
dc03 ansible_host=192.168.121.162 dns_domain=dc03 dict_key=dc03
srv02 ansible_host=192.168.121.92 dns_domain=dc02 dict_key=srv02
srv03 ansible_host=192.168.121.48 dns_domain=dc03 dict_key=srv03

[domain]
dc01
dc02
dc03
srv02
srv03

[dc]
dc01
dc02
dc03

[parent_dc]
dc01
dc03

[child_dc]
dc02

[server]
srv02
srv03

[trust]
dc01
dc02
dc03

[laps_dc]
dc01
dc02
dc03

[laps_server]
srv02
srv03

[adcs]
srv02

[adcs_customtemplates]
srv02

[iis]
srv02
srv03

[mssql]
srv02

[mssql_ssms]
srv02

[webdav]
srv02

[defender_off]
dc01
dc02
dc03
srv02
srv03

[all:vars]
ansible_user=vagrant
ansible_password=vagrant
ansible_connection=winrm
ansible_winrm_server_cert_validation=ignore
ansible_winrm_transport=ssl
ansible_winrm_scheme=https
ansible_port=5986
EOF
Step 2: Resume the MatrixWith dc03 in the correct group, Ansible will run the Main DC playbook on it instead, which will work perfectly.Additionally, because we have wasted a few minutes debugging, dc02 has finally had enough time to initialize its internal DNS records in the background, meaning srv02 will finally be able to ping it and join the domain.Fire the ultimate command.BashANSIBLE_ALLOW_BROKEN_CONDITIONALS=True ansible-playbook -i workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/inventory ansible/main.yml -e "data_path=$PWD/ad/GOAD/data" -e @ad/GOAD/data/config.json -e "force_dns_server=yes" -e "dns_server=8.8.8.8" -e "enable_http_proxy=false" -e '{"keyboard_layouts":["us"]}' -e "add_route=no" -e "install_exchange=no" -e "admin_user=vagrant" -e "admin_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "safemode_password=VagrantP@ssw0rd!" -e "dns_server_forwarder=8.8.8.8"

### Assistant

You are literally at the final boss door. dc03 successfully promoted to a root Domain Controller (ok=31 changed=8)! All three of your Active Directory Domain Controllers are now officially online and communicating.We just have two final puzzle pieces preventing the member servers (srv02 and srv03) from joining their respective domains:The srv03 Auth Error: The user name or password is incorrect. When we overrode the variables, we told Ansible to join the domain using the vagrant user. While vagrant is the local admin, the Domain Admin is the built-in Administrator account.The srv02 DNS Error: The specified domain either does not exist... srv02 is having an identity crisis. It's asking the default NAT router where north.sevenkingdoms.local is instead of asking dc02.We are going to forcefully correct the DNS routing on the servers, switch our auth user to Administrator, and finish this build.Step 1: Force the DNS TargetingRun these two ad-hoc commands. This will reach directly into srv02 and srv03 via PowerShell and forcefully hardcode their DNS servers to point to their respective Domain Controllers.Bash# Point srv02 directly to dc02

Third time is the charm!Since you restarted, the entire network routing matrix, the virtual environment, and the VM states have reset again. We know exactly how to handle this now. Let's do the fast-track Re-entry Protocol, fix the DNS routing on those member servers, and finally finish this build.Step 1: The Fast-Track Re-entry ProtocolCopy and paste this entire block. It will wake up the VMs, drop NordVPN, rebuild your iptables routes to the internet, and reactivate your Python virtual environment all in one shot.Bash# 1. Wake the VMs
cd ~/Desktop/GOAD/workspace/df53f6-goad-libvirt/provider
vagrant up

# 2. Drop the VPN shield
nordvpn disconnect

# 3. Rebuild the routing matrix
sudo sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
MAIN_IF=$(ip route | grep default | awk '{print $5}')
sudo iptables -I FORWARD -m state --state RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -I FORWARD -s 192.168.121.0/24 -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING -s 192.168.121.0/24 -o $MAIN_IF -j MASQUERADE

# 4. Return to base and activate Ansible
cd ~/Desktop/GOAD
source .venv/bin/activate
